sections.title: ENT-M05-L02: Unit economics: what one sale really earns
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Calculate the real profit on one sale or one customer, including materials, delivery, fees, your time and the cost of winning the customer. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour study, 2 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Unit economics** answers one question: when I make one more sale, do I make money? A "unit" is one sale (a cake, a setup, a pack) or one customer over time.

### The key numbers

- **Price:** what the customer pays. If you are registered for GST, use the price without GST.
- **Variable costs:** costs that rise with each sale: ingredients or materials, packaging, delivery fuel, payment fees, platform commissions, wastage.
- **Contribution per unit = price − variable costs.** This is what each sale adds towards your fixed costs and profit.
- **Contribution margin = contribution ÷ price × 100%.**
- **Your time:** hours per unit. **Earnings per hour = contribution ÷ hours.** Compare it with what you could earn another way, such as an hour of tuition.
- **Customer acquisition cost (CAC):** what it costs to win one new customer: free samples, discounts, travel to meet them, ads, referral rewards. **CAC = money spent on winning customers ÷ number of new customers.**
- **Lifetime value (LTV), simple version:** contribution per order × the number of orders a typical customer makes. Use what you actually see, not what you hope.
- **LTV ÷ CAC:** if winning a customer costs more than they will ever contribute, growth makes you poorer. Investors often look for LTV several times bigger than CAC; your rule is simply that LTV must be clearly bigger.

### Hidden costs beginners forget

Wastage and failed batches, gas and electricity, phone data, boxes and stickers, travel to suppliers, payment gateway fees (Razorpay, for example, lists 2% plus GST per transaction on its standard plan; plain UPI into your bank account usually costs less), free extras such as candles and toppers, and the discount you give "just this once".

### Fixed costs come next

Rent, equipment instalments, phone plans and subscriptions don't change with each sale. In Module 8 you will compare them with your contribution to find your break-even point.

## Local example

**Nisha's 1 kg chocolate cake:**

| Item | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Price | 800 |
| Ingredients (flour, cocoa, butter, eggs, cream, sugar) | 310 |
| Gas and electricity | 35 |
| Box and cake board | 40 |
| Candles and topper (free extras) | 15 |
| Delivery fuel (4 km on average) | 30 |
| Wastage allowance (5% of ingredients) | 16 |
| **Variable cost** | **446** |
| **Contribution** | **354** |
| Contribution margin | 44% |

Time: 2.5 hours for baking, decorating and delivery. Earnings per hour: ₹354 ÷ 2.5 = **about ₹142**.

If she gives ₹100 off, her contribution falls to ₹254. A 12.5% cut in price takes away 28% of what she keeps. Discounts cost more than they look.

**Winning customers:** she gives a ₹200 tasting box to a new family, and about half of the boxes lead to an order, so her CAC is about ₹400. A typical family orders 3 cakes a year, so LTV = 3 × ₹354 = ₹1,062. LTV ÷ CAC is about 2.7: tasting boxes pay off, but only if families come back.

**Arun's setup:** price ₹1,500, variable costs ₹150 (bus fares and data), contribution ₹1,350, time 5 hours, so ₹270 an hour. His care plan: ₹500 a month for about 1.5 hours of work, roughly ₹330 an hour, and it repeats every month.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [YC: "Startup Business Models and Pricing" (Aaron Epstein)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWZbWzAyHAE) | Watch the second half, on pricing | about 17 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [a16z: "16 Startup Metrics"](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/) | Read the parts on gross profit, lifetime value (LTV) and customer acquisition cost (CAC) | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 9](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/9-introduction) | Section 9.3 Accounting Basics for Entrepreneurs, for the cost terms | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Razorpay pricing](https://razorpay.com/pricing/) | Only if you will use a payment gateway: the fee per transaction (check current rules) | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Choose your main unit: one cake, one setup, one pack, one CV.
2. Get real prices for every input. Check your receipts, or ask two suppliers by phone or WhatsApp.
3. Time yourself delivering one unit, from start to finish.
4. Fill in the unit economics sheet below: contribution, margin, earnings per hour, CAC and LTV.
5. Write down one change that would improve your numbers (a cheaper supplier, a new price, less wastage, a bundle), and ask a supplier or customer about it this week.

**Proof to record:** Your filled unit economics sheet with real prices, your timing and the improvement you plan.

## Template: unit economics calculator (Unit economics tab)

```csv
Item,Amount per unit (Rs),Notes
Price (without GST if registered),,
Materials or ingredients,,
Packaging,,
Delivery,,
Payment or platform fees,,
Wastage allowance,,
Free extras,,
Variable cost total,=SUM(B3:B8),
Contribution,=B2-B9,
Contribution margin %,=B10/B2*100,
Hours per unit,,
Earnings per hour,=B10/B12,
Spent on winning customers this month,,
New customers this month,,
Customer acquisition cost (CAC),=B14/B15,
Orders per customer per year,,
Lifetime value (LTV),=B10*B17,
LTV divided by CAC,=B18/B16,
```

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting your time.** A cake that earns ₹142 an hour is a business; one that earns ₹40 an hour is a hobby. Always work out earnings per hour.
- **Leaving out small costs.** Boxes, candles, data, fees and wastage add up to a big share of the price. List them all.
- **Treating a discount as normal.** A small price cut takes a big bite out of contribution. Calculate before you discount.
- **Ignoring CAC.** Free samples and travel are real costs of winning customers. If CAC is more than LTV, more customers means more loss.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Price ₹500, variable cost ₹300. What is the contribution?
    - A) ₹800
    - B) ₹200
    - C) ₹300
    - D) ₹500
2. Contribution ₹200 on a price of ₹500. What is the contribution margin?
    - A) 20%
    - B) 40%
    - C) 60%
    - D) 250%
3. You spent ₹1,200 on samples and travel and won 4 new customers. What is your CAC?
    - A) ₹300
    - B) ₹1,200
    - C) ₹4,800
    - D) ₹120
4. Contribution is ₹354 per order and a customer orders 3 times a year. What is the simple LTV?
    - A) ₹354
    - B) ₹1,062
    - C) ₹118
    - D) ₹3,540
5. Which of these is a variable cost?
    - A) A monthly phone plan
    - B) An oven instalment
    - C) Cake boxes
    - D) Shop rent

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the second half of the YC pricing talk, the a16z metrics and OpenStax 9.3 (about 1 hour)
- **Action:** cost out one unit with real prices and your timing, and calculate contribution, CAC and LTV. It is done when your proof is saved: your filled unit economics sheet with real prices, your timing and the improvement you plan.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** ₹500 − ₹300 = ₹200.
2. **B.** ₹200 ÷ ₹500 × 100% = 40%.
3. **A.** ₹1,200 ÷ 4 = ₹300 per customer.
4. **B.** 3 × ₹354 = ₹1,062.
5. **C.** You need one more box for every extra cake; the others stay the same each month.

sections.title: ENT-M05-L03: Set your price with confidence
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Choose a price and 2–3 packages using your costs, the value to the customer and the alternatives, then test them on at least 5 real customers. **Time:** about 4 hours (1 hour study, 3 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Most beginners price too low, out of fear. A low price doesn't make you more competitive if it leaves you exhausted and unable to deliver well. Look at price from three directions.

### 1. The floor: your costs

Your price must cover the variable cost, a share of fixed costs and a fair hourly earning for you. Below the floor, every sale loses money or your time.

**Floor = variable cost per unit + (monthly fixed costs ÷ units a month) + (hours per unit × your target hourly earning)**

### 2. The reference: the alternatives

What does the customer pay for the next-best option, including hidden costs? For Nisha's customers, the Vatakara cake costs ₹900 plus an hour of travel. That is the comparison in their minds.

### 3. The ceiling: the value to the customer

What is solving the problem worth to them? If one extra saree sale a week earns Rasheed ₹600 of profit, a ₹500-a-month care plan pays for itself in the first week. Value-based pricing charges a share of the value you create.

Set your price between the floor and the ceiling, near the reference, and above it if you are clearly better.

### Packages

Offer 2–3 options, so customers choose between your packages instead of between you and someone else:

| Package | Its job |
| --- | --- |
| Basic | The entry price: just the core job |
| Standard (most chosen) | What most people need; mark it as the popular choice |
| Premium | More service or speed; it makes the standard look reasonable |

Spell out exactly what each one includes and what it doesn't. Add-ons (extra photos, rush delivery, an extra revision) let customers pay for what they value.

### Payment terms and promises

- Ask for an **advance** on custom work. 50% before you start is common for cakes and services.
- Accept UPI and give a receipt for every payment.
- State your refund or redo policy before the sale, not after a complaint.
- Show prices clearly. For packed products, India's legal metrology rules require label details such as the MRP (check current rules).

### Test prices with real people

Quote your price confidently, then stop talking and listen. If everyone says yes at once, you may be too cheap. If nobody does, find out whether the problem is the price or the value. Try different prices with similar customers and record each response. Raise prices for new customers first, and give existing customers notice.

### Indian pricing habits

Prices like ₹499 or ₹999 are common, and customers are used to them. Festival offers work, but give them an end date and keep them occasional, or customers learn to wait for the next one.

## Local example

**Arun's price test.** His floor for a setup: ₹150 variable cost + 5 hours × his ₹250 target = ₹1,400. The reference: a nephew does it "for free" but badly, and a Kozhikode agency quoted Rasheed ₹5,000. The ceiling: one extra sale a week is worth more than ₹2,000 a month to a shop.

He offered three packages to 8 shop owners:

| Package | What's included | Price | Chosen by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | WhatsApp Business profile, 5 quick replies, away message | ₹999 | 1 |
| Standard | Basic, plus a 30-item catalogue, labels, Google Business Profile and staff training | ₹1,800 | 4 |
| Premium | Standard, plus 3 months of the care plan | ₹2,900 | 1 |

Two owners said all three were too expensive. Six of the eight bought, at an average of about ₹1,850, more than the ₹1,500 he had planned to charge. Standard became his main offer.

**Meera's CV Makeover** has three packages: ₹499 (CV only), ₹999 (CV and LinkedIn profile, the most chosen) and ₹1,799 (CV, LinkedIn and a 30-minute mock interview on Google Meet). She takes full payment upfront and includes one free revision.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [YC: "Startup Business Models and Pricing" (Aaron Epstein)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWZbWzAyHAE) | Re-watch the pricing part and note three ideas you will try | 15 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 8](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/8-introduction) | Section 8.1 Entrepreneurial Marketing and the Marketing Mix, the part on price | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Steve Blank: "How to Build a Startup" (free Udacity course)](https://www.udacity.com/course/how-to-build-a-startup--ep245) | Lesson "Revenue Model", if you haven't done it | about 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Department of Consumer Affairs: label rules for packaged goods (PDF)](https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/02-Aug-2024.pdf) | Only if you sell packed products: what the label must show (check current rules) | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Calculate your floor, write down the reference price and estimate the ceiling.
2. Design 2–3 packages, listing exactly what is included and excluded, plus any add-ons.
3. Quote them to at least 5 potential customers. Say the price, then wait. Record yes, no or hesitation, and the words they use.
4. Set your launch price list and payment terms: the advance, and your refund or redo policy.
5. Put the price list on a one-page offer sheet (Canva or Google Docs) and into your WhatsApp Business catalogue.

**Proof to record:** Your floor, reference and ceiling numbers, the price test log with 5 or more people, and your one-page price list.

## Template: price calculator and packages

```
PRICE FLOOR
Variable cost per unit: ₹____
+ fixed costs a month ₹____ ÷ units a month ____ = ₹____
+ hours per unit ____ × target ₹____ an hour = ₹____
= FLOOR ₹____

REFERENCE (next-best option, with hidden costs): ₹____
CEILING (value to the customer): ₹____

PACKAGES
Basic ₹____: includes ____ / excludes ____
Standard ₹____ (most chosen): includes ____
Premium ₹____: includes ____
Add-ons: ____ ₹____
Payment terms: ____% advance by UPI, balance on ____
Refund or redo policy: ____________
```

## Template: price test log (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Date,Customer code,Package offered,Price quoted,Response (yes / no / hesitated),Their exact words,Bought? (amount)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Pricing by fear.** Customers judge value partly by price. Set it from the floor, the reference and the value, not from fear of hearing no.
- **Copying the cheapest competitor.** You can't win a price war against a bigger shop. Compete on what your customers care about: trust, speed, quality, language.
- **Too many options.** Five packages confuse people. Two or three are enough.
- **Unclear scope.** "Full setup" means different things to different people. List what is included, or you will do extra work for free.
- **No advance on custom work.** Ask for 50% before you start. It also filters out people who aren't serious.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Variable cost ₹200; fixed costs ₹3,000 a month over 30 units; 1 hour per unit at a ₹150 target. What is the floor?
    - A) ₹200
    - B) ₹300
    - C) ₹450
    - D) ₹350
2. Why offer three packages?
    - A) To confuse customers
    - B) So customers choose between your options instead of between you and a competitor
    - C) The law requires it
    - D) To lower your prices
3. Every customer says yes to your price instantly. What might that mean?
    - A) Your price may be too low
    - B) Your product is bad
    - C) You must lower the price
    - D) Nothing at all
4. What is a sensible payment term for a custom cake order?
    - A) No payment until delivery
    - B) A 50% advance before you start
    - C) Payment after a month
    - D) A free first cake for everyone

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the YC pricing section, OpenStax 8.1 on price and the Steve Blank revenue lesson (about 1 hour)
- **Action:** calculate your floor and ceiling, design packages and test them on at least 5 customers. It is done when your proof is saved: your floor, reference and ceiling numbers, the price test log with 5 or more people, and your one-page price list.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** ₹200 + (₹3,000 ÷ 30 = ₹100) + (1 × ₹150) = ₹450.
2. **B.** Packages also let customers who want more pay more.
3. **A.** Some hesitation is normal at a fair price. Test a higher price with new customers.
4. **B.** An advance covers your ingredients and shows the order is real.

Action: calculate your floor and ceiling, design packages and test them on at least 5 customers

sections.title: Module 6: Marketing
sections.summary: Marketing is how the right people find out about you, understand what you offer and trust you enough to try it. For a small business in Kerala, that happens mostly through WhatsApp, Instagram, YouTube, Google Maps and, above all, people talking to each other.
sections.content:
## Overview

Marketing is how the right people find out about you, understand what you offer and trust you enough to try it. For a small business in Kerala, that happens mostly through WhatsApp, Instagram, YouTube, Google Maps and, above all, people talking to each other.

You don't need an advertising budget. You need a clear position, a simple brand, useful content posted regularly, a complete Google profile and a reason for happy customers to tell others.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Write a positioning statement and choose a name you can legally use
- Build a basic brand kit and a complete WhatsApp Business profile for ₹0–₹500
- Plan and publish two weeks of useful content, following honest disclosure rules
- Create a complete Google Business Profile and a routine for real reviews
- Run an honest referral offer and track where each customer came from

## Time

About 17 hours in total: 16 hours of lessons and 1 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 13–15.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M06-L01: Positioning and low-budget branding (about 5 hours)
2. ENT-M06-L02: Content that sells on WhatsApp, Instagram and YouTube (about 6 hours)
3. ENT-M06-L03: Google Business Profile and local SEO (about 3 hours)
4. ENT-M06-L04: Word of mouth, referrals and reviews (about 2 hours)

## Module project: Marketing kit

1. Your positioning statement, name check results and brand kit (L01).
2. A screenshot of your complete WhatsApp Business profile (L01).
3. Your 14-day content calendar with at least 10 posts published, and their results (L02).
4. Your Google Business Profile, live or waiting for verification, or a note on the channel you use instead (L03).
5. Your referral offer and the Source column in your Customers tab (L04).
6. One paragraph: which channel brought the most replies and orders this month, and what you will do more of.

**Proof to record:** The Founder Toolkit/06 Marketing folder with your brand kit, screenshots, content results and channel summary.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning | "For everyone, best quality" | Clear but generic | A specific customer, category, benefit and proof |
| Name and brand | Not checked | Checked on Google only | Trademark search, handles checked, a simple consistent kit |
| Content | Random offers | Regular posts, mostly offers | Planned pillars, 10 or more posts, replies and orders tracked |
| Local presence | None | A profile with gaps | Complete Google profile and WhatsApp Business, with real reviews |
| Word of mouth | Hoping it happens | Asking sometimes | Referral offer, review routine and source tracking |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: write the positioning statement and complete WhatsApp Business; use your name as plain text instead of a logo.
- L02: post one useful thing a day on WhatsApp Status for 7 days.
- L03: create the Google profile and ask 3 customers for reviews.
- L04: ask your 3 happiest customers for one referral each.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Spending on design before you have customers.** Start with free tools; upgrade from profits.
- **Trying to be on every platform.** Pick the one or two channels where your customers already are.
- **Fake reviews or bought followers.** They break platform rules and trust, and misleading claims can break the law.

tasks.text: Module project: Marketing kit
tasks.detail: **Proof to record:** The Founder Toolkit/06 Marketing folder with your brand kit, screenshots, content results and channel summary.

tasks.text: Self-assessment: rubric scored, no row at 1

sections.title: ENT-M06-L01: Positioning and low-budget branding
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Write a positioning statement, choose a name you can legally use, and build a simple brand kit and WhatsApp Business profile for ₹0–₹500. **Time:** about 5 hours (1.5 hours study, 3.5 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Positioning: the place you hold in a customer's mind

Before any logo, decide what you want people to think when they hear your name. A useful positioning statement:

**For [target customer] who [need], [business name] is the [category] that [key benefit], because [proof]. Unlike [main alternative], we [key difference].**

Small businesses rarely win on price. Choose one or two differences that your interviews showed customers care about:

- **Specialisation:** "only for textile and mobile shops", "only LDC and LGS practice"
- **Speed:** "replies in 5 minutes", "your CV in 48 hours"
- **Local trust:** "your neighbour in Kuttiady", "we come to your shop"
- **Language:** "explained in Malayalam"
- **Quality or values:** "natural colours, no preservatives"
- **Personal service:** "the owner answers your call"

### Choosing a name

A good name is easy to say in Malayalam and English, easy to spell when someone searches for it, not misleading, and not too close to an existing brand. Before you fall in love with a name, check:

1. **Trademark search** on IP India's public search, in the class for your goods or services (cakes and services fall in different classes).
2. **Google and Google Maps:** is there a similar business name nearby?
3. **Instagram, YouTube and Facebook:** is the handle free?
4. **Meaning:** does it mean anything odd in Malayalam, Hindi or Arabic? Many customers have Gulf links.

A name too close to a well-known brand can bring a legal notice and a forced rename after you have printed everything. If you later register a trademark (Module 9), the online filing fee for individuals, startups and small enterprises is ₹4,500 per class, against ₹9,000 for others (check current rules).

### A brand kit for ₹0

- **Logo:** your name in one clear font, plus at most one simple symbol you make yourself. Canva's free licence does not allow content from its library in a logo, trademark or business name, so build your logo from text and shapes you draw.
- **Two colours** (a main colour and an accent) and **one or two fonts**, used everywhere.
- **A tagline** of 3–7 words, taken from your value proposition.
- **A photo style:** real photos of your own work, daylight, a plain background, no stock images.
- **A tone of voice:** friendly, simple and respectful, in both English and Malayalam.

### The same everywhere

Your WhatsApp Business profile, Instagram bio, Google profile, visiting card, stickers, receipts and price list should all use the same name, logo, colours, phone number and one-line description. Consistency is what makes a small business look trustworthy.

## Local example

Nisha first wanted to call her bakery "Kuttiady Cake House". When she searched, she found a bakery with a very similar name in the next town, and similar marks for bakery goods in the trademark search. To avoid confusion and a possible legal problem, she chose **Nisha's Oven**, checked it the same way, and found the Instagram handle @nishasoven.kuttiady free.

Her positioning: "For parents in and around Kuttiady who want a birthday cake they can trust, Nisha's Oven is the home bakery that makes cakes with natural colours and less sugar, because every cake is baked in her own kitchen the day before. Unlike town bakeries, she bakes to order and delivers within 5 km."

Her brand kit cost ₹350, all of it for 200 round stickers from a local printer: the name in a rounded font, a small oven she drew from simple shapes, cream and deep red, the tagline "Baked at home, with care", and photos taken on her balcony in the morning light.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 8](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/8-introduction) | Sections 8.4 Entrepreneurial Branding and 8.3 Marketing Techniques and Tools for Entrepreneurs | 50 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [IP India: search existing trademarks](https://ipindia.gov.in/trade-marks-before-you-apply-search-existing-trademarks) | Open the public search tool and practise with your name ideas (search by word mark) | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Canva Free Media License](https://www.canva.com/policies/free-media) | Read what you may and may not do with free content, especially the logo rule | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [WhatsApp Business app (Google Play listing)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whatsapp.w4b) | Read the features: business profile and catalogue | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Write your positioning statement, using evidence from your interviews.
2. Shortlist 5 names. Check each one: IP India trademark search, Google and Google Maps, Instagram and YouTube handles, and meanings.
3. Test your top 2 names: tell 5 target customers both names, then message them the next day and ask which one they remember.
4. Make a brand kit in Canva from your own text and shapes: logo, two colours, fonts, tagline and three sample photos of your work.
5. Complete your WhatsApp Business profile: logo, description, address or service area, hours, a catalogue with prices, and a greeting or away message.

**Proof to record:** Your positioning statement, the name check table, a screenshot of your brand kit and a screenshot of your complete WhatsApp Business profile.

## Template: positioning statement and name check

```
POSITIONING
For ____ who ____,
[name] is the ____ that ____,
because ____.
Unlike ____, we ____.

NAME CHECK (Y = clear, N = problem)
Name | Trademark | Google/Maps | Instagram | YouTube | Meaning OK | Easy to spell
1.
2.
3.
4.
5.
Remembered the next day by ____ of 5 people
```

## Template: brand kit

```
BRAND KIT
Name: ____________
Tagline (3-7 words): ____________
Main colour: ____  Accent colour: ____ (write the hex codes)
Fonts: ____ for headings, ____ for text
Logo: my own text and shapes, no Canva library elements
Photo style: real work, daylight, plain background
Tone: ____ (for example: friendly, simple, respectful)
One-line description (the same everywhere): ____________
Must appear on: WhatsApp Business, Instagram bio, Google
profile, visiting card, stickers, receipts, price list
```

## Common mistakes

- **Spending thousands on a logo first.** A text logo and two colours are enough to start. Upgrade when customers are paying for it.
- **A name that is hard to spell.** If people can't spell it, they can't search for it. Test it on five people.
- **Copying a famous brand.** Look-alike names and logos invite legal trouble and confuse customers. Search before you print.
- **Stock photos of food or products.** Customers want to see your real work, and stock photos can look dishonest.
- **Different details on every platform.** One name, one number, one description, everywhere.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is the strongest positioning for a small business?
    - A) "Best quality at the lowest price for everyone"
    - B) A specific customer, a clear benefit and a real difference, such as "natural-colour cakes baked to order for Kuttiady parents"
    - C) "We do everything"
    - D) "Cheapest in Kerala"
2. What does Canva's free media licence say about logos?
    - A) Any Canva element can go in your logo
    - B) Content from Canva's library can't be used in a trademark, logo or business name
    - C) All logos made in Canva are free to trademark
    - D) It says nothing about logos
3. What should you check before printing stickers with your name?
    - A) Only Instagram
    - B) The trademark search, Google and Maps, social handles and meanings
    - C) Nothing
    - D) Only what your family thinks
4. Why use the same name, number and description everywhere?
    - A) WhatsApp requires it
    - B) Consistency builds trust and helps people find you
    - C) It is cheaper
    - D) To confuse competitors

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 8.4 and 8.3, the IP India search, Canva's licence and the WhatsApp Business features (about 1.5 hours)
- **Action:** write your positioning, check and test names, build a brand kit and complete your WhatsApp Business profile. It is done when your proof is saved: your positioning statement, the name check table, a screenshot of your brand kit and a screenshot of your complete WhatsApp Business profile.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Specific positioning is believable and easy to remember.
2. **B.** Other people can use the same content, so you can't own it as your mark.
3. **B.** A rename after printing costs money and confuses customers.
4. **B.** Matching details look professional and make searching easy.

Action: write your positioning, check and test names, build a brand kit and complete your WhatsApp Business profile

sections.title: ENT-M06-L02: Content that sells on WhatsApp, Instagram and YouTube
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Plan and publish two weeks of useful content on one or two channels, using content pillars, a simple calendar and honest disclosure, and track which posts bring replies and orders. **Time:** about 6 hours (1 hour 40 minutes study, 4 hours 20 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Content marketing** means helping, teaching or showing first, and selling second. People buy from businesses they know and trust, and useful content builds that trust before you ask for money.

### Choose one or two channels

| Channel | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WhatsApp Status and catalogue | Local customers who have your number | The highest trust in Kerala towns. Broadcast lists reach only people who have saved your number. |
| WhatsApp channel or group | Regular updates for followers | Ask before you add anyone to a group. |
| Instagram (professional account) | Things that look good: food, design, fashion, places | Reels, Stories, location tags, a link in your bio. |
| YouTube Shorts and videos | Teaching: tips, how-tos, explanations | Searchable for years; good for digital products. |
| Facebook groups | Older audiences and local communities | Follow each group's rules. |

Start where your customers already are; your interviews told you where. Two channels done well beat five done badly.

### Four content pillars

Plan posts around four themes:

1. **Show:** your product and process. A cake being decorated, a shop's new catalogue, the first page of a practice pack.
2. **Teach:** a useful tip. "3 ways to store a cream cake", "how to answer WhatsApp enquiries faster", "5 PSC questions on Kerala's rivers".
3. **Prove:** results and real reviews, shared with the customer's permission.
4. **Personal:** your story and values. Why you started, a day of your work, a lesson you learned.

A good rhythm is about three helpful posts for every offer, and always a clear way to order or get in touch.

### Make it on a phone

- **Hook in the first 2 seconds:** start with the result or a question, not your logo.
- **Keep it short:** 15–45 seconds for Reels and Shorts.
- **Natural light** and a steady phone (lean it on something). Use real sound or music from the app's own library.
- **Captions** in Malayalam or English, because many people watch with the sound off.
- **One call to action:** "WhatsApp 98XXXXXXXX to order" or "Link in bio".
- **Batch it:** shoot 6–8 short clips in one 2-hour session, then post them through the week.

### Stay honest and legal

- Use only photos, music and clips you made or have the right to use. Never take photos from Google.
- If you pay someone to promote you, give them free products, or have any other connection with them, the post must say so clearly. ASCI's guidelines list labels such as #ad, #collaboration and #sponsored, placed where viewers can't miss them.
- Never post fake reviews or invented before-and-after results. Misleading ads can break consumer protection law.

### Measure what matters

For each post, note the views, the replies or messages, and the orders. After two weeks, do more of what brought replies and orders, not of what got the most likes.

## Local example

Nisha's first week on WhatsApp Status and Instagram:

| Day | Pillar | Post |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mon | Show | A 20-second Reel of a rainbow cake being decorated with natural colours |
| Tue | Teach | "Why my red colour comes from beetroot" (photo with text) |
| Wed | Prove | A customer's thank-you message, shared with permission |
| Thu | Show | This week's flavours and prices, with the catalogue link |
| Fri | Personal | "Baking since I was 12, in my mother's kitchen" (photo) |
| Sat | Offer | "Weekend orders close tonight at 8 pm" |
| Sun | Teach | "How to cut a cake neatly" (a 15-second clip) |

Results: 7 posts, about 900 Status views, 140 Instagram views, 19 messages and 6 orders. Five of the six orders came after the Monday Reel and the Thursday price list, so in week two she posted two process Reels and kept the price list on Thursdays.

**Fathima** posts one PSC question a day as a YouTube Short, with the answer explained in Malayalam in 30 seconds, ending with "The full weekly test is free in our WhatsApp channel". **Arun** posts before-and-after screenshots of shops' WhatsApp catalogues, with the owners' permission.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [HubSpot Academy: Content Marketing (free course)](https://academy.hubspot.com/courses/content-marketing) | Free sign-up. Do the first 2 lessons (the whole course is about 8 hours 20 minutes) | about 1 hour | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [YouTube Creators (free guides)](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) | Open the "Get started" and Shorts guides | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Instagram help: set up a professional account](https://help.instagram.com/502981923235522) | If you use Instagram: set up a professional account | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [ASCI: influencer advertising FAQs](https://www.ascionline.in/social/faqs/) | Read which disclosure labels to use and where to put them | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Choose one or two channels, based on where your interviewees said they spend their time.
2. Write your four content pillars, with three post ideas for each.
3. Plan 14 days of posts in the content calendar below.
4. Batch-shoot and publish at least 7 posts in the first week, and keep posting in the second week.
5. Track views, replies and orders for every post. Write down which two posts worked best, and why you think they did.

**Proof to record:** Your 14-day calendar, links or screenshots of at least 7 published posts, and the results table.

## Template: 14-day content calendar (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Date,Channel,Pillar (show / teach / prove / personal / offer),Hook (first 2 seconds),Post idea,Call to action,Views,Replies,Orders
```

## Template: hooks and captions

```
HOOKS (the first 2 seconds)
- Show the result first: the finished cake, the full catalogue
- Ask a question: "Losing customers at night on WhatsApp?"
- Use a number: "3 CV mistakes that cost you interviews"
- Before and after
- "Watch this before you order a birthday cake"

CAPTION
Line 1: the hook again, in words
Lines 2-3: one useful point, or the story
Line 4: the call to action (how to order or contact you)
Hashtags: 3-5 local and topic tags
(#Kuttiady #Kozhikode #homebakery #KeralaPSC)

CALL TO ACTION IN MALAYALAM
ഓർഡർ ചെയ്യാൻ WhatsApp ചെയ്യൂ: [നമ്പർ]
കൂടുതൽ വിവരങ്ങൾക്ക് ബയോയിലെ ലിങ്ക് നോക്കൂ.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Only posting offers.** Constant "buy now" posts get muted. Help, show and prove first.
- **Posting irregularly.** Ten posts in one day and then nothing for a month builds no trust. Plan and batch.
- **Chasing followers.** A thousand followers outside your area are worth less than fifty local parents. Track replies and orders.
- **Using other people's photos or music.** It can get posts removed and accounts flagged, and it breaks trust. Use your own.
- **No call to action.** Every post needs a clear next step: how to order or contact you.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which mix of helpful posts and offers is a good starting rhythm?
    - A) All offers
    - B) About 3 helpful posts to every offer
    - C) Never post an offer
    - D) 10 offers to every helpful post
2. Who receives your WhatsApp broadcast messages?
    - A) Everyone in your contacts
    - B) Only people who have saved your number
    - C) Everyone on WhatsApp
    - D) Only groups
3. You gave an Instagram creator a free cake to post about. What must the post include?
    - A) Nothing
    - B) A clear disclosure label such as #ad or #collaboration, where viewers can't miss it
    - C) Your phone number
    - D) A discount code
4. Which number best tells you a post worked?
    - A) Likes
    - B) The replies and orders it brought
    - C) New followers
    - D) The number of hashtags

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** two HubSpot content lessons, the YouTube Creators guides, Instagram's professional account help and ASCI's labels (about 1 hour 40 minutes)
- **Action:** plan 14 days of content on one or two channels, publish at least 7 posts and track replies and orders. It is done when your proof is saved: your 14-day calendar, links or screenshots of at least 7 published posts, and the results table.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Helpful posts earn the attention that makes offers work.
2. **B.** That is why asking customers to save your number matters.
3. **B.** A free product is a material connection under ASCI's guidelines.
4. **B.** Replies and orders are actionable; likes are vanity numbers.

sections.title: ENT-M06-L03: Google Business Profile and local SEO
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Create or claim a free Google Business Profile, complete every section accurately, and set up a weekly routine for photos, posts and real reviews. **Time:** about 3 hours (40 minutes study, 2 hours 20 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

When someone in Kuttiady searches "cake shop near me" or "mobile repair Vatakara", Google shows a map with a few businesses. A **Google Business Profile** is the free listing that puts you on that map and in Google Search. Google says creating one costs nothing.

### Can you have one?

Business Profiles are for businesses that meet customers in person: either customers come to you (a shop, or a home bakery with pickup) or you go to them (delivery, on-site service). If you work from home and don't want your address shown, list a **service area** (for example Kuttiady, Thottilpalam and Vatakara) and hide the address. A business that sells only online, such as a digital product, usually doesn't qualify; use WhatsApp, Instagram or YouTube instead.

### How Google ranks local results

Google's help page says local results depend mainly on three things:

- **Relevance:** how well your profile matches the search. Pick the right primary category and describe what you actually offer.
- **Distance:** how far you are from the person searching, or from the place in their search.
- **Prominence:** how well known you are, including your reviews and how often others mention and link to you.

You can't change distance, but you can improve relevance and prominence.

### A complete profile

- **Name:** your real business name, exactly as on your board. Don't add keywords such as "Best Cakes Kuttiady" to the name; it breaks Google's guidelines and can get the profile suspended.
- **Category:** the most specific primary category, plus a few secondary ones.
- **Contact:** phone or WhatsApp number, and a website or Instagram link.
- **Hours:** accurate, including holidays.
- **Address or service area.**
- **Products or services, with prices.**
- **Description:** what you offer, to whom and where, in plain words that people actually search for ("home-made birthday cakes in Kuttiady").
- **Photos:** at least 10 real ones: products, work in progress, you, and the outside of the shop if you have one. Add new photos every week.

### Reviews: ask, never fake

Ask every happy customer for an honest review, right after they thank you. Make it easy: send your review link or show a QR code at the counter. Reply to every review, good or bad, politely and within a few days. Never write reviews yourself, pay for them or give gifts only for five-star ratings. Fake reviews break Google's rules and destroy trust when they are found out.

### The same details everywhere

Use exactly the same name, address and phone number on Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, any directory such as JustDial, and your printed material. Mismatched details confuse customers and search engines alike.

## Local example

Arun claimed Rasheed's existing listing, which had the wrong hours and no photos. He chose the most specific shop category, added 25 real photos, the WhatsApp number, the hours (including Sunday closing) and a description: "Sarees, salwar sets and kids' wear on Kuttiady main road, near the bus stand. New stock every week. WhatsApp us for photos and prices." He printed a QR code linking to the review page and placed it at the billing counter.

In the following month, the shop received 12 reviews from real customers, averaging 4.7 stars, and the calls and direction requests shown in the profile's performance page both went up.

Nisha, who bakes at home, listed Nisha's Oven as a service-area business covering Kuttiady and nearby places, with her home address hidden.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Google Business Profile help: a free Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7039811) | Read what a free Business Profile includes and who can have one | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Google Business Profile help: improve your local ranking](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en) | Read how relevance, distance and prominence work | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Google Skillshop (free training)](https://skillshop.withgoogle.com/) | Optional: look for the free Business Profile training | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Decide whether your business qualifies (customers come to you, or you serve them in your area). If it doesn't, write down which channel you will use instead, and do the steps below for that channel.
2. Create or claim your profile and complete the verification Google asks for.
3. Fill in every section using the checklist below, and add at least 10 real photos.
4. Ask 5 real customers for honest reviews with the message below. Reply to every review.
5. Put a 15-minute weekly Google routine in your calendar: a new photo, a post, and replies to reviews and questions.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your complete profile (or of the channel you chose instead), your review requests and the weekly routine in your calendar.

## Template: profile checklist

```
GOOGLE BUSINESS PROFILE CHECKLIST
[ ] Business name exactly as on the board (no extra keywords)
[ ] Most specific primary category, plus 2-3 secondary
[ ] Phone or WhatsApp number (the same as everywhere else)
[ ] Website or Instagram link
[ ] Hours, including holidays
[ ] Address shown, or service area with the address hidden
[ ] Products or services with prices
[ ] Description: what, for whom, where, in plain words
[ ] 10 or more real photos (products, work, you, outside)
[ ] Review link or QR code ready
[ ] Weekly 15 minutes: a photo, a post, replies
```

## Template: review requests and replies

```
REVIEW REQUEST (right after a happy customer says thanks)
Thank you so much! If you liked it, could you write a short,
honest review on Google? It really helps a small business
like mine: [review link]

MALAYALAM
വളരെ നന്ദി! ഇഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടെങ്കിൽ, ഗൂഗിളിൽ ഒരു ചെറിയ
സത്യസന്ധമായ റിവ്യൂ എഴുതാമോ? എന്നെപ്പോലുള്ള ഒരു
ചെറിയ സംരംഭത്തിന് അത് വലിയ സഹായമാണ്: [ലിങ്ക്]

REPLY TO A BAD REVIEW
Thank you for telling us, [name]. I'm sorry about [issue].
I'd like to put it right. Please WhatsApp me on [number].
```

## Common mistakes

- **Stuffing keywords into the business name.** "Nisha's Oven Best Cakes Kuttiady" breaks Google's guidelines. Put the keywords in the description instead.
- **Fake or paid reviews.** They break Google's rules and, once discovered, destroy the trust your business depends on. Ask real customers.
- **Wrong hours.** A customer who arrives at a closed shutter won't come back. Keep holiday hours up to date.
- **Showing your home address by accident.** If you work from home, choose a service area and hide the address.
- **Ignoring bad reviews.** A calm, helpful reply to a complaint shows future customers that you care.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which three factors does Google name for local ranking?
    - A) Price, size and age
    - B) Relevance, distance and prominence
    - C) Followers, likes and shares
    - D) Ads, budget and logo
2. Nisha bakes at home and delivers. What should she do about her address?
    - A) Hide it and list a service area
    - B) Use a fake shop address
    - C) Not create a profile at all
    - D) Put it in the business name
3. Which business name follows Google's guidelines?
    - A) "Nisha's Oven"
    - B) "Nisha's Oven Best Birthday Cakes Kuttiady Cheap"
    - C) "Cakes Near Me"
    - D) "No. 1 Bakery Kerala"
4. What should you do after a bad review?
    - A) Delete your profile
    - B) Reply calmly, apologise for the problem and offer to fix it
    - C) Argue in public
    - D) Ask friends for fake five-star reviews

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the two Google Business Profile help pages, plus Skillshop if you have time (about 40 minutes)
- **Action:** create or claim your Google Business Profile, complete it, ask 5 customers for reviews and set a weekly routine. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your complete profile (or of the channel you chose instead), your review requests and the weekly routine in your calendar.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Those are the three factors on Google's own help page.
2. **A.** Service-area businesses can hide their address and show the areas they serve.
3. **A.** Use your real name only; keywords belong in the description.
4. **B.** Future customers read your reply as much as the complaint.

sections.title: ENT-M06-L04: Word of mouth, referrals and reviews
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Design a simple, honest referral offer, ask happy customers for referrals at the right moment, and track where every customer comes from. **Time:** about 2 hours (35 minutes study, 1 hour 25 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

In Kerala towns, most new customers come from people talking to each other: family groups, neighbours, colleagues, people waiting at the bus stop. Word of mouth is free, but it doesn't happen by itself. You can make it more likely.

### Give people something to talk about

- **A remarkable moment:** something a little better than expected. A handwritten note, a free cupcake for the birthday child, a WhatsApp reply in two minutes, a call a week later to check everything is working.
- **Something easy to share:** a photo-worthy product, a short message that is ready to forward, a visiting card with a QR code.
- **A story:** "the young man from Kuttiady who set up our shop's WhatsApp" is easy to repeat.

### Ask at the happy moment

The best time to ask for a referral or a review is right after the customer says "thank you" or "it's perfect". Be specific: "Do you know one other shop owner who struggles with WhatsApp enquiries?" is easier to answer than "Please tell everyone".

### A simple referral offer

**Give-get:** the new customer gets something, and so does the person who referred them. For example ₹50 off for both, a free add-on, or one free month of care for every new shop referred.

Rules that keep it honest:

- Reward referrals that become paying customers, not sign-ups.
- Keep it to one level. Rewards for the referrals of your referrals start to look like a pyramid scheme, and India's Direct Selling Rules prohibit promoting pyramid and money-circulation schemes.
- Never pay for reviews, and never make a reward depend on a five-star rating.

### Be present in the community

Local events, markets and partnerships spread the word fast: a stall at a Kudumbashree market or a local festival (with the organisers' permission), a small prize at a school event, or cross-promotion with a business that has the same customers (cakes with a party decorator, CVs with a nursing coaching centre).

### Track where every customer comes from

Ask every new customer, "How did you hear about us?", and write the answer in the Source column of your Customers tab. After a month you will know which channel deserves your time.

## Local example

Nisha slips a small card into every cake box: "Loved your cake? Share this card. Your friend gets ₹50 off their first order, and you get ₹50 off your next one. WhatsApp 98XXXXXXXX." She asks for a Google review the moment a customer sends a thank-you message. In her first month of tracking, her 26 new customers came from referral cards (9), WhatsApp Status (7), Instagram (4), family groups (3) and a stall at a Christmas market (3).

Arun gives an existing client one free month of the care plan (worth ₹500) for every new shop they refer that buys a setup. In the first month, two shop owners referred their brothers' shops in Vatakara.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Paul Graham: "Do Things That Don't Scale"](https://paulgraham.com/ds.html) | Re-read the part about delighting your first users | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 8](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/8-introduction) | Section 8.6 Sales and Customer Service | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules, 2021 (UNEP LEAP law database)](https://leap.unep.org/en/countries/in/national-legislation/consumer-protection-direct-selling-rules-2021) | Note that pyramid and money-circulation schemes are prohibited (check current rules) | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Design one "remarkable moment" you can afford to give every customer.
2. Write a give-get referral offer and make a referral card or message (Canva or plain text).
3. Ask your 5 happiest customers, at the happy moment, for one referral or one honest review each.
4. Add a Source column to your Customers tab, and ask every new customer how they heard about you.
5. Plan one community activity for next month: a market stall, an event or a partner business.

**Proof to record:** Your referral card or message, your 5 asks and what happened, and a Source column with at least 5 entries.

## Template: referral card, referral ask and source codes

```
REFERRAL CARD (visiting-card size)
Loved it? Share this card.
Your friend gets ____ off their first order,
and you get ____ off your next one.
Order: WhatsApp [number]
[Business name] | [tagline]

ASKING FOR A REFERRAL (at the happy moment)
I'm so glad you liked it! Do you know one other
[parent / shop owner / nurse] who might need this?
If you share my number, you both get ____.

MALAYALAM
ഇഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടതിൽ വളരെ സന്തോഷം! ഇത് ആവശ്യമുള്ള
മറ്റൊരാളെ അറിയാമോ? എന്റെ നമ്പർ അവർക്ക്
കൊടുത്താൽ, നിങ്ങൾക്ക് രണ്ടുപേർക്കും ____ കിട്ടും.

SOURCE CODES (Customers tab)
REF = referral card   WA = WhatsApp Status
IG = Instagram        YT = YouTube
G = Google            GRP = group
EVT = event           PART = partner
OTH = other
```

## Common mistakes

- **Asking too late.** A week later, the excitement has gone. Ask right after the thank-you.
- **Complicated rules.** If your referral offer needs a paragraph, nobody will use it. One sentence, two rewards.
- **Multi-level rewards.** Rewards for referrals of referrals drift towards a pyramid scheme. Keep it to one level.
- **Spamming groups.** Posting the same offer in every group annoys people and gets you removed. Ask the admins, and add value first.
- **Not tracking sources.** Without a Source column, you can't tell which effort is working.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. When is the best time to ask for a referral?
    - A) Before delivery
    - B) Right after the customer says thank you
    - C) A month later
    - D) Never
2. Which referral offer is the safest?
    - A) Rewards for every level of referrals below you
    - B) A one-level give-get: the new customer and the referrer each get a small reward
    - C) Paying for five-star reviews
    - D) A joining fee
3. Why ask, "How did you hear about us?"
    - A) As small talk
    - B) To track which channels bring customers
    - C) To collect data to sell
    - D) The law requires it
4. Of 26 new customers, 9 came from referral cards and 7 from Status. What should Nisha do?
    - A) Stop the referral cards
    - B) Keep and improve the cards and Status, and review the weaker channels
    - C) Start paying for ads
    - D) Change nothing

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** "Do Things That Don't Scale" (the part on delight), OpenStax 8.6 and the Direct Selling Rules note (about 35 minutes)
- **Action:** create a referral offer, ask 5 happy customers for referrals or reviews and start tracking sources. It is done when your proof is saved: your referral card or message, your 5 asks and what happened, and a Source column with at least 5 entries.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** That is when the customer feels best about you.
2. **B.** One level keeps it simple and clearly away from pyramid schemes.
3. **B.** Source tracking tells you where to spend your limited time.
4. **B.** Put more effort into what works, and fix or drop what doesn't.

Action: create a referral offer, ask 5 happy customers for referrals or reviews and start tracking sources

sections.title: Module 7: Sales
sections.summary: Marketing makes people aware of you; sales turns interested people into paying customers. For a small business, sales is mostly honest conversations: finding the right people, asking good questions, making a clear offer, handling doubts and following up.
sections.content:
## Overview

Marketing makes people aware of you; sales turns interested people into paying customers. For a small business, sales is mostly honest conversations: finding the right people, asking good questions, making a clear offer, handling doubts and following up.

This module gives you a pipeline, scripts in English and Malayalam, an objection playbook and a follow-up system. Your target by the end of week 18: 50 sales conversations logged, and paying customers who are not friends or family.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Build a list of 50 prospects and run a daily outreach habit with a simple pipeline
- Use tested scripts for WhatsApp, phone, walk-ins and email, and set up one partnership
- Handle common objections calmly, ask for the sale clearly and collect payment with written terms
- Follow up so that no lead is forgotten, and ask for reviews and referrals after delivery

## Time

About 17 hours in total: 15 hours of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 16–18.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M07-L01: Get your first 10 customers (about 6 hours)
2. ENT-M07-L02: Outreach scripts and partnerships (about 5 hours)
3. ENT-M07-L03: Handle objections, close and follow up (about 4 hours)

## Module project: Sales kit and results

1. Your adapted scripts (L02) and objection playbook (L03), in one document.
2. Your Customers tab with at least 50 prospects and every conversation logged (L01).
3. One partnership with written terms (L02).
4. Your numbers: conversations, offers, sales and the conversion rate at each step.
5. Your top 5 reasons for "no", and what you will change because of them.

**Proof to record:** The sales kit document in Founder Toolkit/07 Sales, plus your Customers tab.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pipeline | No list | A list, but no stages or dates | 50 or more prospects, with stages, next steps and dates |
| Outreach | Mass messages | Personal, but irregular | Personal, a daily habit, with follow-ups |
| Scripts | None | Written, not tested | Tested, reply rates compared, improved |
| Objections and closing | Argue or discount | Answer some objections | Playbook used, a clear ask, payment terms in writing |
| Results | No sales | Sales to friends and family only | Paying customers who are not friends or family |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: list 25 prospects and contact 10.
- L02: use one WhatsApp script and one follow-up.
- L03: prepare answers to your top 3 objections.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Waiting for customers to come.** Reach out personally, every day, even if only to three people.
- **Mass messaging strangers.** Send personal messages to the right people instead.
- **Giving up after one message.** Most sales need several polite follow-ups.

sections.title: ENT-M07-L01: Get your first 10 customers
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a list of 50 prospects, run daily outreach with a simple pipeline, and close paying customers who are not friends or family. **Time:** about 6 hours (1 hour study, 5 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Sales is helping the right people decide. Your first customers won't find you by chance; you go to them. Paul Graham's "Do Things That Don't Scale" makes the point plainly: early on, founders recruit customers one at a time, by hand.

### Where the first 50 prospects come from

1. **People you interviewed**, and anyone who joined your waiting list in Module 4.
2. **Your second-degree network:** ask 10 friends and relatives for one introduction each.
3. **Walk-ins:** shops, offices, clinics and coaching centres near you, at quiet hours.
4. **Communities:** online and offline groups where your customers gather, within their rules.
5. **Partners:** businesses that serve the same customers (next lesson).

### Qualify before you pitch

A good prospect has four things. Check them gently in conversation:

- **Problem:** they have the problem now.
- **Budget:** they can pay your price.
- **Decision:** they decide, or you can talk to the person who does.
- **Timing:** they want it solved soon, not "maybe next year".

### Your pipeline

Track every prospect through these stages in your Customers tab:

**Prospect → Contacted → Conversation → Offer sent → Won (paid) or Lost → Delivered → Repeat or referral**

Every open prospect needs a **next step** and a **date**. A pipeline without dates is just a list.

### The numbers, honestly

Sales is partly a numbers game. An early funnel might look like this (an illustration, not a promise): 50 prospects → 25 replies → 12 conversations → 6 offers → 3 sales. Your rates will be different, so measure them. If 6 in every 100 prospects buy and you want 10 more customers, you need about 170 more prospects, or a better conversion rate.

### A daily habit beats a big push

Part-time: 3 new contacts each weekday evening, plus visits or calls at the weekend. Full-time: 10–15 a day. Small, steady effort keeps the pipeline full.

### Respect people and the rules

Send personal messages, not copy-pasted blasts. Don't add people to groups without asking. When someone says no, stop. WhatsApp can restrict accounts that send bulk unwanted messages, and pestering people ruins your name in a small town.

## Local example

By week 16 Arun has 10 paying shops: 4 pilots from Module 4 and 6 from his price test. His goal is 30 by the end of the course.

His new list of 50 prospects: 22 shops from earlier conversations, 14 introductions from friends, uncles and existing clients, and 14 walk-in targets on the main roads of Kuttiady, Thottilpalam, Nadapuram and Vatakara. His habit: three WhatsApp messages or calls each weekday evening after PSC study, and a two-hour walk-in round on Saturday late mornings, when most owners have time to talk.

After two weeks: 50 prospects → 31 replied or met him → 17 real conversations → 9 offers → 5 sales (three Standard, two Basic). Three of the five were people he had never met before. His conversion from prospect to sale was 10%, so to win 15 more shops he needs about 150 more prospects, or a better close rate. That is what the next two lessons work on.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [YC: "How to Get Your First Customers" (Gustaf Alströmer)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hyYCn_kAngI) | Watch the whole talk | about 23 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [HubSpot: Inbound Sales training (free)](https://www.hubspot.com/sales/sales-training) | Free. Start the Inbound Sales course with its first class | about 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Do Things That Don't Scale"](https://paulgraham.com/ds.html) | Re-read the part on recruiting users by hand | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Build your list of 50 prospects in the Customers tab, using the five sources above.
2. Mark what you already know about each one: problem, budget, decision and timing.
3. Contact at least 25 of them this week with personal messages, calls or visits. A short opener is enough for now; the next lesson gives full scripts.
4. Log every contact: its stage, the next step and the date.
5. Aim for 3 or more real conversations and at least 1 paid sale to someone who is not a friend or family member. Count how many prospects are at each stage.

**Proof to record:** The Customers tab with 50 prospects, at least 25 contacts logged with next steps, and your stage counts.

## Template: pipeline (Customers tab)

```csv
Code,Name,Phone (with consent),Source,Problem? (Y/N),Budget? (Y/N),Decides? (Y/N),Timing,Stage,Last contact,Next step,Next date,Offer,Value (Rs),Paid (Rs),Notes
P01,,,REF,,,,,Prospect,,,,,,,
```

## Template: daily outreach tracker

```
DAILY OUTREACH (part-time: 3 a day; full-time: 10-15 a day)
Date: ____
New contacts: 1. ____ 2. ____ 3. ____
Follow-ups due today: ____
Conversations booked: ____
Offers sent: ____  Sales: ____  Amount: ₹____
One thing I learned: ____________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Waiting for customers to come to you.** Posting and hoping is not selling. Reach out personally every day.
- **Mass messaging.** One personal message beats fifty copy-pasted ones, and blasts can get your WhatsApp restricted.
- **Selling to people who can't buy.** Check problem, budget, decision and timing before you spend hours on someone.
- **No next step.** Every conversation should end with an agreed next step and a date.
- **Counting only friends.** Friends and family are welcome customers, but they don't prove the business works. Track strangers separately.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which four things does a qualified prospect have?
    - A) Name, age, phone and address
    - B) The problem, a budget, the power to decide and the right timing
    - C) Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and email
    - D) A shop, a car, a house and land
2. If 5% of your prospects buy, how many prospects do you need for 10 customers?
    - A) 20
    - B) 50
    - C) 200
    - D) 500
3. What must every open prospect in your pipeline have?
    - A) A discount
    - B) A next step and a date
    - C) A gift
    - D) A signed contract
4. Why track sales to strangers separately from sales to friends and family?
    - A) Friends don't pay
    - B) Sales to strangers show the business works without personal favours
    - C) They are taxed differently
    - D) WhatsApp requires it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the YC first-customers talk, the first HubSpot sales class and the PG essay (about 1 hour)
- **Action:** build a 50-prospect pipeline, contact 25 and win a paying customer who is not a friend. It is done when your proof is saved: the Customers tab with 50 prospects, at least 25 contacts logged with next steps, and your stage counts.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Without all four, a sale is unlikely however good your offer is.
2. **C.** 10 ÷ 0.05 = 200. A better conversion rate means fewer prospects.
3. **B.** Dates turn a list into a pipeline you can act on.
4. **B.** Strangers buy only because the offer is worth it.

Action: build a 50-prospect pipeline, contact 25 and win a paying customer who is not a friend

sections.title: ENT-M07-L02: Outreach scripts and partnerships
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use short, tested scripts for WhatsApp, phone, walk-ins and email, follow up on a schedule, and set up one partnership that sends you customers. **Time:** about 5 hours (1 hour 20 minutes study, 3 hours 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A script is not something to recite. It is a tested structure that keeps you clear and brief. Good outreach has five parts:

1. **A personal opener:** who you are and how you know of them ("Rasheed from the textile shop gave me your number").
2. **The reason:** why you are contacting this particular person.
3. **The value:** the problem you solve or the result, in one sentence, with proof if you have it.
4. **A small ask:** 10 minutes, a visit, a demo, a sample. Not "buy now".
5. **An easy exit:** "If it's not useful, no problem at all." People relax when they know they can say no.

### Tips for each channel

- **WhatsApp text:** under 60 words, ending with a question.
- **WhatsApp voice note:** common and personal in Kerala. Keep it under 30 seconds, speak slowly, then send a one-line text summary.
- **Phone call:** first ask, "Is this a good time for 2 minutes?"
- **Walk-in:** go at quiet hours, carry your one-page offer sheet, and leave a card or a sample.
- **Email:** for offices, schools and professionals. A clear subject line and three short paragraphs.

### Follow up

Most people don't reply to a first message because they are busy, not because they aren't interested. A polite schedule:

- **Day 0:** your first message
- **Day 2–3:** a short follow-up with something useful (a tip, a photo of a result)
- **Day 7:** a check-in offering a specific time
- **Day 14:** a last, friendly message: "I'll stop here so I don't disturb you. If it's ever useful, my number is ____."

Then stop, mark them "Lost: no reply" and move on.

### Partnerships: customers who come to you

A **partner** is a business that already serves your customers but doesn't compete with you:

| Your business | Good partners |
| --- | --- |
| Home bakery | Party decorators, photographers, event halls, gift shops |
| WhatsApp setup for shops | Mobile shops, printing shops, tax practitioners' offices, billing software sellers |
| PSC practice packs | Libraries, tuition centres, teachers with YouTube channels, stationery shops near colleges |
| CV service | Nursing and engineering coaching centres, language institutes, properly licensed recruitment agencies |

Common ways to partner: a **referral fee** (for example 10% of the first order), a **bundle** (their product with yours), **co-marketing** (you promote each other) or **white-label** (you deliver under their name).

Write the terms down in a short note or message that both of you confirm: what each side does, the fee and when it is paid, how referrals are tracked, and how either side can end it.

Choose partners carefully. A partner who makes wild promises damages your name, and for anything involving overseas jobs, deal only with properly licensed agencies: fake job offers are a common scam. Never let a partner promise customers anything that isn't in your offer sheet.

## Local example

Arun tested two WhatsApp openers on 20 shops each:

- **A:** "Hi, I help shops with WhatsApp Business. Interested?" got 3 replies out of 20 (15%).
- **B:** "Hi Ramesh, Rasheed from the textile shop on Kuttiady main road told me you get a lot of WhatsApp enquiries in the evenings. I set up his WhatsApp Business so customers get photos and prices in minutes; two customers ordered from his catalogue without coming in. Can I show you on your phone for 10 minutes on Saturday? If it's not useful, no problem." got 11 replies out of 20 (55%).

He kept B. He also agreed a partnership with a printing shop in Kuttiady that sells visiting cards and shop boards: the printer recommends ShopAssist to new shops and receives ₹200 for each one that buys a setup. They wrote the terms in one WhatsApp message and both replied "agreed". In the first month, the printer sent three shops and two bought.

Nisha agreed a similar arrangement with a party decoration shop: the decorator suggests her cakes when families book a birthday, and she pays 10% of each cake order that comes through them.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [HubSpot: Inbound Sales training (free)](https://www.hubspot.com/sales/sales-training) | Continue the Inbound Sales course: the classes on connecting with and exploring prospects | about 1 hour | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 12](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/12-introduction) | Section 12.1 Building and Connecting to Networks | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Adapt the scripts below to your business, in English and Malayalam.
2. Use each script at least 5 times this week, and track the reply rate for each one in your Customers tab.
3. Follow up every open prospect on the schedule: day 2–3, day 7 and day 14.
4. List 5 possible partners, and propose a partnership to at least 2 of them, in person or by phone.
5. Agree one partnership with written terms. A WhatsApp message that both of you confirm is enough to start.

**Proof to record:** Your adapted scripts, the reply rate for each script, and the written terms of your partnership.

## Template: outreach scripts and follow-ups

```
WHATSAPP (under 60 words)
Hi [name], [who referred you / how I know you]. I help
[type of customer] with [problem]. [One proof: a result
or a customer]. Could I show you in 10 minutes on [day]?
If it's not useful, no problem at all.

MALAYALAM
നമസ്കാരം [പേര്], [ആര് പറഞ്ഞിട്ട് / എങ്ങനെ അറിയാം].
[ഉപഭോക്താക്കൾക്ക്] [പ്രശ്നം] പരിഹരിക്കാൻ ഞാൻ സഹായിക്കുന്നു.
[ഒരു ഫലം]. [ദിവസം] 10 മിനിറ്റ് കാണിച്ചുതരട്ടെ?
ഉപകാരമില്ലെങ്കിൽ ഒരു പ്രശ്നവുമില്ല.

PHONE
"Hello [name], this is [your name] from [place]. Is this
a good time for 2 minutes? ... [reason and value] ...
Could I visit on [day] at [time] to show you?"

WALK-IN
"Namaskaram, I'm [name]. I help [type] shops with
[problem]. Is the owner free for 5 minutes now, or is
there a better time?" Leave your offer sheet.

EMAIL
Subject: [result] for [their business]
Paragraph 1: who you are, and why you are writing to them
Paragraph 2: the result you get, with one proof
Paragraph 3: a small ask, with two time options

FOLLOW-UPS
Day 2-3: "Sharing a quick example: [photo or tip]."
Day 7: "Would Saturday 11 am or Monday 4 pm suit you?"
Day 14: "I'll stop here so I don't disturb you. If it's
ever useful, my number is [number]. Thank you!"
```

## Template: partnership note

```
PARTNERSHIP NOTE (both sides confirm by message)
Partners: [you] and [partner]
What [partner] does: recommends us to ____
What we do: ____ (for example: recommend them, bundle)
Fee: ____ (for example 10% of the first order, or ₹200
per paying customer), paid by ____ within ____ days
Tracking: the customer says "[partner] sent me" or uses
the code ____
Promises to customers: only what is in our offer sheet
Either side can end this with ____ days' notice
Start date: ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Long messages.** Nobody reads a paragraph from a stranger. Keep WhatsApp messages under 60 words.
- **Talking about yourself.** Lead with their problem and the result, not your life story.
- **No clear ask.** End with one small, specific request: a day and a time.
- **Giving up after one message.** Follow up three times over two weeks, politely, then stop.
- **Partnerships on a handshake only.** Write the terms in one message that both sides confirm, so nobody is surprised later.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which opener is likely to work better?
    - A) "Interested in my service?"
    - B) A personal opener naming who referred you, the result you get and a small ask with a specific time
    - C) A 300-word message
    - D) A forwarded poster with no text
2. A prospect hasn't replied to your first message. What should you do?
    - A) Never contact them again
    - B) Follow up politely on day 2–3, day 7 and day 14, then stop
    - C) Message them every day
    - D) Add them to a group
3. Which is a good partner for a home bakery?
    - A) Another home baker on the same street
    - B) A party decoration shop
    - C) A tyre shop
    - D) A bank
4. What should a written partnership note cover, at least?
    - A) Only the start date
    - B) What each side does, the fee and when it is paid, tracking, and how to end it
    - C) Nothing, trust is enough
    - D) The partner's family details

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the HubSpot classes on connecting and exploring, and OpenStax 12.1 (about 1 hour 20 minutes)
- **Action:** test outreach scripts, follow up on schedule and agree one written partnership. It is done when your proof is saved: your adapted scripts, the reply rate for each script, and the written terms of your partnership.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Personal, specific and easy to say yes to. In Arun's test it got 55% replies against 15%.
2. **B.** Busy people often reply to the second or third message. Stop after the fourth.
3. **B.** Same customers at the same moment, and no competition.
4. **B.** Clear terms keep good partners and avoid arguments.
