sections.title: ENT-M07-L03: Handle objections, close and follow up
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Respond calmly to common objections, ask for the sale clearly, collect payment with written terms, and set a follow-up for every open lead. **Time:** about 4 hours (45 minutes study, 3 hours 15 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

An objection is usually a question or a worry in disguise. "It's too expensive" often means "I'm not sure it's worth it" or "I can't pay it all at once". Your job is to understand, not to win an argument.

### A simple method: LAER

1. **Listen** to the whole objection without interrupting.
2. **Acknowledge** it: "That's a fair question."
3. **Explore** what is behind it: "When you say expensive, compared with what?"
4. **Respond** with facts, proof or an option, then check: "Does that answer your worry?"

### Common objections and calm responses

| What they say | What it may mean | A calm response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "വില കൂടുതലാണ്" (it's too expensive) | Not sure it's worth it, or short of cash | "Compared with what? ... One extra sale a month covers it. We can also start with the Basic package." |
| "I'll think about it" | A worry they haven't said | "Of course. So I can help, what's the main thing you're unsure about?" |
| "I need to ask my husband / my son in Dubai" | A shared decision | "Good idea. Shall I send a 1-minute voice note you can forward, or join a call with both of you?" |
| "My nephew can do it" | Price, or doubt about the value | "That can work. The difference is ____, and I support you every month. Would a trial help you compare?" |
| "Send the details on WhatsApp" | A polite brush-off, or real interest | "Sure. So I send the right thing, which part matters most to you?" Then agree a time to follow up. |
| "I tried this before and it didn't work" | A bad past experience | "What happened? ... Here is what we do differently, and here is my money-back promise." |
| "Not now. After Onam." | Timing | "Understood. Shall I call on [date]? Here's one free tip until then." |

### Ask for the sale

Many beginners never actually ask. When the customer's questions have been answered, ask clearly:

- **Summary close:** "So: catalogue, quick replies and the Google profile for ₹1,800, set up this Saturday. Shall we go ahead?"
- **Choice close:** "Would the Basic or the Standard package suit you better?"
- **Trial close:** "Would you like to try it for two weeks with the money-back promise?"
- **Real deadline:** "The festival price ends on Sunday." Use it only if it is true.

Then be quiet and let them answer.

### Collect payment and put the terms in writing

- Take the advance by UPI and send a receipt the same day.
- Send a short written summary: what is and isn't included, the price, the date, the payment terms and your refund or redo policy. A WhatsApp message is enough for small jobs; for bigger ones, use the simple agreement in Module 9.

### Follow up after the sale, and after a no

Check in after delivery ("Is everything working well?"), then ask for a review and a referral at the happy moment (ENT-M06-L04). After a "no", ask politely: "Can I ask what made you decide not to?" Reasons for losing are valuable data.

### Never pressure or deceive

No false deadlines, no fake scarcity, no promises you can't keep, and no pushing people who have said no. In a small town, one pushy sale can cost you ten future customers.

## Local example

Arun visited a mobile shop in Thottilpalam:

**Owner:** "₹1,800? Too much. My nephew can do it."
**Arun:** "That's fair; a nephew is a good option. Can I ask how many WhatsApp enquiries you get on a busy day?"
**Owner:** "Maybe 30. He only comes on Sundays."
**Arun:** "So on weekdays, who replies?"
**Owner:** "Nobody, until I close."
**Arun:** "That's the gap I fix. Rasheed in Kuttiady had two catalogue orders in his first week. If one extra phone sale a month covers the cost, would it be worth trying? I can do the Basic package for ₹999 now, and you can upgrade later."
**Owner:** "Okay, Basic. But what if it doesn't work?"
**Arun:** "Then I refund you within 14 days. Shall I set it up on Saturday at 11?"

He took a ₹500 advance by UPI, sent a receipt and a WhatsApp summary of what was included, and set a reminder to follow up a week after the setup. Two months later, the owner upgraded to the Standard package and joined the care plan.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [HubSpot: Inbound Sales training (free)](https://www.hubspot.com/sales/sales-training) | Finish the Inbound Sales classes on advising and closing | about 45 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. List the 5 objections you hear most often, using the notes in your Customers tab.
2. Write a calm LAER response to each one in the playbook below, in English and Malayalam.
3. Role-play with a friend or family member: they raise each objection and you respond. Record it on your phone and listen back once.
4. Use the playbook in real conversations this week. Ask for the sale clearly whenever the customer's questions have been answered.
5. Make sure every open lead has a next step and a date. For every "no", ask the reason and record it.

**Proof to record:** Your objection playbook, the role-play recording, and at least 1 closed sale or 5 recorded reasons for "no".

## Template: objection playbook and closing lines

```
OBJECTION PLAYBOOK
Objection 1: "____"
  What it may mean: ____
  Question to explore: ____
  Response: ____
  Proof or option: ____
(repeat for objections 2-5)

CLOSING LINES
Summary: "So: ____ for ₹____, starting ____.
Shall we go ahead?"
Choice: "Would ____ or ____ suit you better?"
Trial: "Would you like to try it for ____ with my
money-back promise?"

AFTER A NO
"Thank you for your time. Can I ask what made you
decide not to? It helps me improve."
```

## Template: order confirmation

```
ORDER CONFIRMATION (send on WhatsApp after the yes)
Thank you, [name]! Here is what we agreed:
Included: ____
Not included: ____
Price: ₹____
Advance received: ₹____ on ____ (UPI ref ____)
Balance: ₹____ due on ____
Delivery or setup date: ____
Refund or redo policy: ____
Questions any time: [number]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Arguing.** Proving the customer wrong loses the sale. Ask what is behind the objection instead.
- **Discounting at the first objection.** Offer a smaller package or a trial before you cut the price.
- **Never asking for the sale.** If you don't ask, many people won't decide. Ask clearly, then stay quiet.
- **Nothing in writing.** A short written summary prevents "I thought it included…" arguments later.
- **Forgetting lost leads.** Ask why, record it, and check in again when timing was the reason.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. A customer says, "I'll think about it." What is a good response?
    - A) "Okay, bye."
    - B) "Of course. What's the main thing you're unsure about?"
    - C) Offer 50% off immediately
    - D) Argue with them
2. In LAER, what does the "E" stand for?
    - A) Escape
    - B) Explore
    - C) Explain loudly
    - D) End
3. Which of these is a choice close?
    - A) "Would the Basic or the Standard package suit you better?"
    - B) "Buy now or regret it"
    - C) "Only 1 left!" when it isn't true
    - D) "Let me know"
4. Why send a written order confirmation?
    - A) The law requires one for every sale
    - B) It records what was agreed, so there are no disputes later
    - C) To look busy
    - D) To collect personal data

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the HubSpot classes on advising and closing (about 45 minutes)
- **Action:** build an objection playbook, role-play it, use it in real sales and log a reason for every no. It is done when your proof is saved: your objection playbook, the role-play recording, and at least 1 closed sale or 5 recorded reasons for "no".
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** It uncovers the real worry so you can answer it.
2. **B.** Exploring finds out what is behind the objection.
3. **A.** It asks for a decision between two good options, without pressure.
4. **B.** Clear terms protect both you and the customer.

sections.title: Module 8: Money and finance
sections.summary: Money is where many small businesses quietly fail: profit on paper but an empty bank account, sales growing but nobody knows where the money went, a tax question nobody expected. This module gives you the money skills every founder needs: simple books, a cash forecast, a profit and loss statement, break-even, beginner-level GST and income tax, and safe ways to fund growth.
sections.content:
## Overview

Money is where many small businesses quietly fail: profit on paper but an empty bank account, sales growing but nobody knows where the money went, a tax question nobody expected. This module gives you the money skills every founder needs: simple books, a cash forecast, a profit and loss statement, break-even, beginner-level GST and income tax, and safe ways to fund growth.

You don't need to become an accountant. You need to record every rupee, look at the numbers every week, and know when to ask a professional.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Keep a daily cash book with receipts and invoices, separate from your personal money
- Make a 13-week cash flow forecast and see a cash crunch coming before it arrives
- Prepare a monthly profit and loss statement and calculate break-even
- Explain when GST registration applies and how presumptive income tax works, and keep a tax calendar
- Choose funding that fits your stage, from customer advances to Mudra and Kerala schemes, and avoid dangerous debt

## Time

About 17 hours in total: 15 hours of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 19–21.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M08-L01: Bookkeeping and cash flow (about 5 hours)
2. ENT-M08-L02: Profit and loss, and break-even (about 3 hours)
3. ENT-M08-L03: Tax basics: GST and income tax for small businesses (about 3 hours)
4. ENT-M08-L04: Funding: bootstrapping, loans, schemes, grants and investors (about 4 hours)

## Module project: Finance sheet

1. Your cash book with 4 weeks of entries and receipts (L01).
2. Your 13-week cash forecast (L01).
3. Your monthly P&L and break-even calculations (L02).
4. Your tax readiness checklist and tax calendar (L03).
5. Your funding plan with the options compared (L04).
6. Review it with someone who keeps accounts (a CA, an accountant friend or a shopkeeper who files GST) and note their comments.

**Proof to record:** Your finance sheet (one Google Sheets file with these tabs) in Founder Toolkit/08 Money, with the reviewer's comments.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Records | Mixed with personal money | Recorded, with gaps | Every rupee for 4 weeks, receipts saved, separate account |
| Cash forecast | None | One month ahead | 13 weeks ahead, updated weekly |
| P&L and break-even | None | Revenue only | A full monthly P&L, break-even and target units |
| Tax | Unaware | Know GST exists | Threshold and compulsory cases checked, calendar set, a professional asked |
| Funding | Borrow when short | Options listed | Options compared on cost and risk, using official sources |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: record every transaction for 2 weeks and skip the forecast for now.
- L02: a P&L for one month and break-even units only.
- L03: check the GST threshold and the compulsory cases.
- L04: write your funding need and two options.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Mixing personal and business money.** Use one account and one QR code for the business.
- **Confusing profit with cash.** Keep both a cash book and a P&L, and look at both.
- **Borrowing before demand is proven.** Fund growth from customers' money first.

sections.title: ENT-M08-L01: Bookkeeping and cash flow
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Keep simple, honest books from day one, with a separate account, a daily cash book, receipts and invoices, and make a 13-week cash flow forecast. **Time:** about 5 hours (1 hour 10 minutes study, 3 hours 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Why keep books from day one

- You can see whether the business really makes money.
- You spot problems early: a supplier's price rise, a customer who never pays.
- Banks and schemes ask for records before they lend.
- Filing tax is easy when records exist, and stressful when they don't.

### Four simple habits

1. **Separate the money.** Use one bank account only for the business. A savings account in your own name is fine at the start; you may need a current account once you register or grow (ask your bank). Take UPI payments into this account only.
2. **Record every rupee, every day.** In the Cashbook tab: date, description, category, money in, money out, payment mode and a receipt link. Cash counts too.
3. **Keep proof.** Photograph every bill and receipt and save it in a Drive folder for that month. Give customers a receipt or invoice for every sale.
4. **Review weekly.** Every Sunday, spend 20 minutes checking that your balance matches the bank and looking at what came in and went out.

### Invoices

An invoice is the bill you give a customer. Include your business name and contact, an invoice number (in order: 001, 002…), the date, the customer's name, what was sold, quantity, price, total, payment received and any balance due. A GST-registered business needs a GST invoice with more details, such as its GSTIN; check the GST portal or ask a tax professional when you get there.

### Cash flow is not profit

**Profit** is revenue minus costs over a period. **Cash flow** is the actual money moving in and out, and when. A profitable business can still run out of cash when:

- customers pay late or buy on credit
- you buy a big stock of ingredients before a festival
- equipment instalments fall due before the season's sales come in

Credit ("pattu" or "kadam") is common in Kerala shops. Set clear rules before you give any: who gets credit, how much and for how long.

### The 13-week cash forecast

For each week: **opening cash + money expected in − money expected out = closing cash.** Plan 13 weeks ahead, about three months. Any week where closing cash falls below zero, or below a small safety amount, is a warning. Chase payments, delay a purchase or ask for advances, before the week arrives.

### Tools

- **Google Sheets** on the phone or laptop, with the templates below.
- **LibreOffice Calc** on the laptop, which works offline.
- **GnuCash**, free and open source, on the laptop only, if you want proper double-entry accounts; its documentation includes a tutorial.

Start simple. A sheet you update every day beats accounting software you open once a month.

## Local example

Nisha's cash book for one week in November:

| Date | Description | Category | In (₹) | Out (₹) | Mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 Nov | Advance for a chocolate cake (Anju) | Sales | 400 | | UPI |
| 3 Nov | Flour, cocoa, butter, cream | Ingredients | | 1,240 | UPI |
| 4 Nov | Balance for the chocolate cake (Anju) | Sales | 400 | | Cash |
| 5 Nov | Boxes and boards, pack of 20 | Packaging | | 600 | Cash |
| 6 Nov | Two vanilla cakes (a school teacher) | Sales | 1,300 | | UPI |
| 7 Nov | Petrol for deliveries | Delivery | | 200 | Cash |
| 8 Nov | Recharge for the business number | Phone | | 299 | UPI |
| 9 Nov | Red velvet cake (an office party) | Sales | 950 | | UPI |
| | **Total** | | **3,050** | **2,339** | |

Money in minus money out: ₹711 for the week. But the 20 boxes and the big stock of flour will last several weeks, so her real profit for the week is higher than the change in cash. That difference is exactly why she also needs a profit and loss statement (next lesson).

Her 13-week forecast showed a problem in December: about ₹9,000 of Christmas ingredients and boxes had to be bought before most Christmas orders were paid. Her fix: a 50% advance on every Christmas order, collected before she buys the ingredients.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 9](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/9-introduction) | Section 9.3 Accounting Basics for Entrepreneurs | 40 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [GnuCash documentation](https://www.gnucash.org/docs.phtml) | Optional, laptop only: the first chapters of the Tutorial and Concepts Guide | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [NCFE: National Centre for Financial Education (free e-learning)](https://ncfe.org.in/) | Optional: the e-learning module on money and transactions | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Choose the bank account you will use only for the business, and make sure your UPI QR code pays into it.
2. Set up the Cashbook tab with the template below. Type your opening balance in H2; in H3 type =H2+D3-E3 and copy it down. Record every transaction for 7 days, including cash, and photograph every receipt into a Drive folder named for the month.
3. Make an invoice template and give one to every customer this week.
4. Build your 13-week cash forecast. In J2 type =B2+C2+D2+E2-F2-G2-H2-I2; next week's opening cash (B3) is =J2.
5. Mark any week where cash falls below ₹500 (or your own safety amount), and write down what you will do about it.

**Proof to record:** Seven days of cash book entries with receipt links, an invoice you sent, and your 13-week forecast with any warning weeks marked.

## Template: cash book (Cashbook tab)

```csv
Date,Description,Category,Money in (Rs),Money out (Rs),Mode (UPI / cash / bank),Receipt link,Running balance
,Opening balance,,,,,,
```

## Template: invoice

```
INVOICE No. ____             Date: ____
From: [business name], [address], [phone]
To: [customer name], [phone]

Item | Qty | Price (₹) | Amount (₹)
____ | ___ | ________ | _________
____ | ___ | ________ | _________
Total: ₹____
Paid: ₹____ (UPI ref ____ / cash) on ____
Balance due: ₹____ by ____
Thank you!
(Once you are GST-registered, use a GST invoice format.)
```

## Template: 13-week cash forecast (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Week starting,Opening cash,In: sales,In: advances,In: other,Out: stock,Out: bills,Out: loan or EMI,Out: other,Closing cash
```

## Common mistakes

- **Mixing personal and business money.** Use one account and one UPI QR code for the business only. Pay yourself a fixed amount instead of dipping in.
- **Not recording cash.** Cash sales and small purchases are the ones that go missing. Write them down the same day.
- **Giving credit without rules.** Decide who can buy on credit, how much and for how long, before anyone asks.
- **Ignoring small fees.** Payment fees, recharges and packaging add up. Record them all.
- **Throwing away receipts.** A photo in a monthly Drive folder takes five seconds and saves hours at tax time.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why use a separate bank account for the business?
    - A) Banks require it of everyone
    - B) So you can see what the business earns and spends
    - C) To avoid tax
    - D) To get loans faster
2. When can a profitable business still run out of cash?
    - A) When customers pay late or you buy stock before sales come in
    - B) When prices are high
    - C) When it has many customers
    - D) When it keeps records
3. Opening cash is ₹2,000, money in ₹5,000 and money out ₹6,500. What is the closing cash?
    - A) ₹500
    - B) ₹13,500
    - C) ₹1,500
    - D) −₹500
4. How should invoice numbers run?
    - A) Randomly
    - B) In order, without gaps
    - C) As the customer's phone number
    - D) As the date only

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 9.3, plus GnuCash or NCFE if you have time (about 1 hour 10 minutes)
- **Action:** set up a business account and cash book, record 7 days, send invoices and build a 13-week cash forecast. It is done when your proof is saved: seven days of cash book entries with receipt links, an invoice you sent, and your 13-week forecast with any warning weeks marked.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Separate money gives you clear numbers, which also helps with loans and tax.
2. **A.** Timing matters: money out can come before money in.
3. **A.** ₹2,000 + ₹5,000 − ₹6,500 = ₹500.
4. **B.** Numbers in order make records easy to check, for you and for any tax officer.

sections.title: ENT-M08-L02: Profit and loss, and break-even
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Prepare a monthly profit and loss statement from your records and calculate your break-even point in units and rupees. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour 10 minutes study, 1 hour 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The profit and loss statement (P&L)

A P&L shows whether you made a profit over a period, usually a month:

| Line | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Revenue** | All sales in the month (without GST, if you are registered) |
| − **Cost of goods sold** | Variable costs of what you sold: ingredients, packaging, delivery |
| = **Gross profit** | What sales contribute before fixed costs |
| − **Operating expenses** | Fixed costs: phone, rent, subscriptions, equipment, marketing |
| = **Operating profit** | Profit from running the business |
| − **Interest and tax** | Loan interest, and income tax set aside |
| = **Net profit** | What is truly left |

Two adjustments keep your P&L honest:

- **Stock bought for later**, such as a bag of flour that lasts a month, is a cost when you *use* it, not when you buy it. A simple way: at the end of the month, estimate the stock left and subtract it from that month's purchases.
- **Equipment** that lasts years, such as an oven or a ring light, loses value slowly. Spread its cost: a ₹12,000 oven expected to last 4 years costs about ₹250 a month. This is **depreciation**.

**Pay yourself.** If your "profit" exists only because you work for free, it isn't really profit. Always compare net profit with the hours you worked.

### Break-even

The **break-even point** is the level of sales where revenue just covers all costs, so profit is zero.

- **Break-even units = monthly fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit**
- **Break-even revenue = monthly fixed costs ÷ contribution margin**
- **Units for a target profit = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit**

Then compare with reality. Can you make and sell that many units a month? This is where capacity (your time, your oven, your delivery radius) shows up.

### What-if checks

Try three changes in your sheet: price down 10%, costs up 10% and sales down 20%. If any one of them wipes out your profit, the business is fragile; look for ways to raise the contribution or cut fixed costs.

## Local example

**Nisha's P&L for November:**

| Line | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue (24 cakes at an average of ₹780) | 18,720 |
| Ingredients used | 7,440 |
| Gas and electricity | 840 |
| Packaging | 960 |
| Delivery fuel | 720 |
| **Gross profit** | **8,760** |
| Phone and data | 300 |
| One Instagram boost (a test) | 200 |
| Oven depreciation (₹12,000 over 4 years) | 250 |
| Interest on the mixer instalment | 120 |
| **Net profit before tax** | **7,890** |

She worked about 60 hours, so she earned roughly ₹130 an hour.

**Break-even:** her fixed costs are ₹870 a month, and her average contribution is ₹365 a cake (₹8,760 ÷ 24). Break-even = ₹870 ÷ ₹365, so 3 cakes a month. Her goal of ₹15,000 net profit a month needs (₹870 + ₹15,000) ÷ ₹365, which is about 44 cakes a month, or 11 a week.

**Capacity check:** her oven bakes 2 cakes at a time, and each cake takes about 2.5 hours of her time. Eleven cakes a week is about 27 hours, too much next to her family duties. Her options: raise prices, sell more high-margin items such as cupcake boxes, or find a part-time helper for decorating (Module 12).

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 9](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/9-introduction) | Section 9.4 Developing Startup Financial Statements and Projections | 40 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 9](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/9-introduction) | Section 9.1 Overview of Entrepreneurial Finance and Accounting Strategies | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Build last month's P&L from your cash book (or this month's so far) with the template below.
2. Adjust for stock bought for later, and add depreciation for any equipment.
3. Calculate your break-even units and revenue, and the units you need for your target monthly profit.
4. Do a capacity check: the hours and equipment those units need. Can you do it?
5. Run the three what-if checks. Choose one change (price, cost or volume) and act on it this week, for example by quoting a new price to a customer or asking a supplier for a bulk rate.

**Proof to record:** Your P&L, break-even and target calculations, the capacity check, the what-if results and the change you made.

## Template: P&L and break-even (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Line,Amount (Rs)
Revenue,
Cost of goods sold: materials used,
Cost of goods sold: packaging,
Cost of goods sold: delivery,
Cost of goods sold: other variable,
Gross profit,=B2-B3-B4-B5-B6
Operating expenses: phone and internet,
Operating expenses: rent,
Operating expenses: marketing,
Operating expenses: depreciation,
Operating expenses: other fixed,
Operating profit,=B7-B8-B9-B10-B11-B12
Interest,
Tax set aside,
Net profit,=B13-B14-B15
Hours worked this month,
Net profit per hour,=B16/B17
Units sold,
Contribution per unit,=B7/B19
Fixed costs this month,=B8+B9+B10+B11+B12+B14
Break-even units,=B21/B20
Target profit,
Units for target profit,=(B21+B23)/B20
```

## Common mistakes

- **Confusing cash with profit.** A good cash week can hide a loss, and a bad one can hide a profit. Use both the cash book and the P&L.
- **Forgetting your own time.** Net profit per hour shows whether the business is worth your effort. Work it out every month.
- **Putting a whole stock purchase into one month.** Count stock as a cost when you use it, or estimate what is left at month end.
- **Ignoring capacity.** A break-even that needs more hours than you have is a warning, not a plan.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Revenue ₹20,000, cost of goods sold ₹9,000 and operating expenses ₹3,000. What is the operating profit?
    - A) ₹11,000
    - B) ₹8,000
    - C) ₹17,000
    - D) ₹32,000
2. Fixed costs are ₹2,000 a month and the contribution is ₹250 a unit. How many units to break even?
    - A) 4
    - B) 8
    - C) 250
    - D) 2,250
3. A ₹24,000 machine lasts 4 years. Roughly how much depreciation is that a month?
    - A) ₹500
    - B) ₹2,000
    - C) ₹6,000
    - D) ₹24,000
4. Your target needs 40 hours a week of work, but you have 6. What does that tell you?
    - A) Work harder
    - B) The plan doesn't fit your capacity: change the price, the product mix or costs, or get help
    - C) Ignore it
    - D) Borrow money

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 9.4 and 9.1 (about 1 hour 10 minutes)
- **Action:** build a monthly P&L, calculate break-even and target units, check capacity and act on one change. It is done when your proof is saved: your P&L, break-even and target calculations, the capacity check, the what-if results and the change you made.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** ₹20,000 − ₹9,000 = ₹11,000 gross profit; minus ₹3,000 = ₹8,000.
2. **B.** ₹2,000 ÷ ₹250 = 8 units.
3. **A.** ₹24,000 ÷ 48 months = ₹500.
4. **B.** Capacity is a real limit. Change the plan rather than burn out.

sections.title: ENT-M08-L03: Tax basics: GST and income tax for small businesses
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Check whether GST registration applies to you, understand presumptive income tax at a basic level, set up a tax calendar and know when to ask a professional. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour 10 minutes study, 1 hour 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Important:** this lesson is general information, checked on 24 October 2026. Tax law changes often: India's new Income-tax Act, 2025 applies to income from 1 April 2026, and GST rules and rates are revised regularly. Before you register, file or decide anything, check the official sources and talk to a chartered accountant or tax practitioner.

### GST: do you need to register?

GST registration depends mainly on your **aggregate turnover** in a financial year (April to March): your total sales, not your profit.

| Your situation in Kerala | Turnover threshold for registration (check current rules) |
| --- | --- |
| You supply only goods | ₹40 lakh a year (a few goods, such as ice cream, pan masala and tobacco, don't get this higher limit) |
| You supply services, or both goods and services | ₹20 lakh a year |

Kerala uses the ₹40 lakh limit for goods because it is not one of the states left out of Notification 10/2019-Central Tax.

**Some businesses must register even below these limits.** The law lists compulsory cases, including certain inter-state supplies of goods and some sales through e-commerce platforms. If you plan to ship goods to other states, or sell on Amazon, Flipkart or Meesho, check the current rules on the GST portal or with a professional before you start.

**If you are not registered, you must not charge GST** or show it on your bills.

**Voluntary registration** is allowed. It can help if your customers are GST-registered businesses that want GST invoices, but it brings regular returns and costs, so don't register "just in case" without advice.

**The composition scheme** is a simpler option for small registered businesses: goods suppliers with turnover up to ₹1.5 crore, and service providers up to ₹50 lakh (at 6% for services), pay tax at a fixed low rate and file less often. They can't charge GST to customers or claim input tax credit (check current rules).

### Income tax: your business income is your income

As a sole proprietor, your business profit is part of your personal income. You file an income tax return (ITR) each year, and the normal slab rates for individuals apply. Even when your income is below the taxable limit, a filed return builds a record that banks and loan schemes often ask for.

**Presumptive taxation, Section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025**, is a simpler scheme for small businesses and professionals; it replaced sections 44AD and 44ADA of the old Act. According to the Income Tax Department's pages (check current rules):

- **Eligible businesses** (resident individuals, HUFs and partnership firms other than LLPs) with turnover up to **₹2 crore**, or up to **₹3 crore** if cash receipts are no more than 5% of turnover, can declare profit as **8% of turnover received in cash and 6% of turnover received through banking or digital channels such as UPI**, or more if their real profit is higher.
- **Specified professions** (such as legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy and interior decoration, plus others listed or notified) with receipts up to **₹50 lakh** (₹75 lakh if cash receipts are no more than 5%) can declare **50%** of receipts as profit.
- Presumptive taxpayers can pay all their advance tax in one instalment by **15 March**.
- If you claim a lower profit than the presumptive rate and your income is above the basic exemption limit, you must keep books and have them audited.

Whether your work counts as a business or as a profession (Arun's setup service or Meera's CV writing, for example) changes the rules, so ask a tax professional.

### Other things to know

- **TDS:** business clients sometimes deduct tax at source before paying you. It isn't lost: it appears in your Annual Information Statement (AIS) on the income tax e-filing portal, and you claim it in your return.
- **Professional tax:** in Kerala, local bodies collect professional tax from people in trades and professions above certain income levels. Ask your panchayat or municipality.
- **Records:** keep your cash book, invoices and receipts for several years.

### When to get professional help

When you approach a GST threshold, when a compulsory case might apply, when you form a partnership, LLP or company, when you hire staff, or whenever you aren't sure. A local tax practitioner's fee is small compared with the cost of a mistake.

## Local example

**Nisha** expects about ₹2.5 lakh of cake sales this year. She supplies only goods, far below the ₹40 lakh threshold, and none of the compulsory cases applies because she sells only locally and directly to customers. She doesn't register for GST and doesn't show GST on her bills. She plans to file an income tax return, using her cash book as the record. Most of her money comes by UPI, so under presumptive taxation the minimum profit she would declare is 6% of her UPI receipts plus 8% of her cash receipts. Her real profit is much higher than that, so she would declare the real figure. Whether she owes any tax depends on her total income and the current slab rates, which she will check with a local tax practitioner before filing.

**Arun** expects about ₹6 lakh this year from setups and care plans, below the ₹20 lakh threshold for services. One client, a larger GST-registered mobile shop, asked for GST invoices; Arun explained that he isn't registered, and the client accepted a normal invoice. He set a reminder to review GST if his turnover passes ₹15 lakh, and asked a CA whether his work counts as a business or a profession for presumptive tax.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [GST Council, 32nd meeting: thresholds and composition scheme (PDF)](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-10/32nd_gst_press_information_bureau.pdf) | Read the decisions on the threshold and the composition scheme | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Notification 10/2019-Central Tax: ₹40 lakh threshold for goods (PDF)](https://www.gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-05/notfctn-10-central-tax-english-2019.pdf) | Read the conditions and the list of states left out (Kerala is not on it) | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [GST portal](https://www.gst.gov.in/) | Browse the help topics on registration (check current rules) | 15 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Income Tax Department: Section 58, Income-tax Act 2025 (presumptive taxation)](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-58-138) | Read the table of who is eligible, the limits and the rates | 15 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Income Tax Department: FAQs on presumptive taxation (PDF)](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/faqs-on-tax-on-presumptive-taxation-scheme) | Read the questions on eligibility and advance tax | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Estimate your turnover for the next 12 months, month by month, from your price list and expected sales.
2. Compare it with the GST threshold for your type of supply, and check the compulsory cases on the GST portal (inter-state supplies, e-commerce sales). Write your answer: register now, not yet, or ask a professional.
3. Read the presumptive taxation limits. Write down which category you might fall into, and the question you need a professional to answer.
4. Fill in the tax readiness checklist, and add a tax calendar to Google Calendar: the ITR due date, the advance tax date, and GST dates if you are registered.
5. Ask one tax practitioner or CA one specific question, by phone or in person. Record the answer and the date.

**Proof to record:** Your 12-month turnover estimate, your GST decision with reasons, the tax checklist, the calendar entries and the professional's answer.

## Template: tax readiness checklist and calendar

```
TAX READINESS CHECKLIST (check current rules on the official sites)
Expected turnover, next 12 months: ₹____
Type of supply: goods only / services / both
GST threshold that applies: ₹____ lakh
Compulsory registration cases that might apply:
[ ] Inter-state supply of goods
[ ] Selling through an e-commerce platform
[ ] Other: ____
GST decision: register now / not yet / ask a professional
If not registered: no GST on my bills [ ]
PAN [ ]   Business bank account [ ]
Income tax: presumptive (Section 58) or regular books? ____
Category: business / specified profession / not sure
Question for my tax professional: ____________
Answer, and the date: ____________

TAX CALENDAR (add to Google Calendar)
Advance tax (presumptive): by 15 March
Income tax return: due date for my category ____
GST returns (if registered): ____
Turnover against the threshold: review every 3 months
```

## Common mistakes

- **Charging "GST" without being registered.** It isn't allowed. If you aren't registered, your bills must not show GST.
- **Watching profit instead of turnover.** GST thresholds are about total sales, not profit. Track turnover every month.
- **Missing the compulsory cases.** Selling on e-commerce platforms or across state borders can require registration even when you are small. Check before you start.
- **Not filing a return because income is low.** A filed return is useful proof of income for loans and schemes. Ask a professional whether you should file.
- **Relying on old rules.** Tax rules change. Check the official sources every year, and note the date you checked.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What are GST registration thresholds based on?
    - A) Profit
    - B) Aggregate turnover in a financial year
    - C) The number of customers
    - D) Your bank balance
2. In Kerala, what is the general threshold for a business that supplies only goods? (Check current rules.)
    - A) ₹10 lakh
    - B) ₹20 lakh
    - C) ₹40 lakh
    - D) ₹1 crore
3. An unregistered business shows "GST 18%" on its bills. Is that right?
    - A) Yes, always
    - B) No: an unregistered business must not charge GST
    - C) Only for cakes
    - D) Only in December
4. Under Section 58 presumptive taxation, what is the deemed profit on business turnover received through UPI or banking channels?
    - A) 50%
    - B) 8%
    - C) 6%
    - D) 0%
5. When should you talk to a tax professional?
    - A) Never
    - B) When you near a threshold, a compulsory case might apply, you change structure or hire, or you aren't sure
    - C) Only after a notice arrives
    - D) Only if you earn crores

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the GST Council decisions, Notification 10/2019, the GST portal's registration help and the two Income Tax Department pages (about 1 hour 10 minutes)
- **Action:** estimate turnover, decide on GST, set a tax calendar and ask a tax professional one question. It is done when your proof is saved: your 12-month turnover estimate, your GST decision with reasons, the tax checklist, the calendar entries and the professional's answer.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Total sales count, even if your profit is small.
2. **C.** Kerala uses the ₹40 lakh limit for goods; services have a ₹20 lakh limit.
3. **B.** Only registered businesses can collect GST.
4. **C.** 6% for banking and digital receipts and 8% for cash; 50% applies to specified professions.
5. **B.** A short consultation early is cheaper than fixing a mistake later.

sections.title: ENT-M08-L04: Funding: bootstrapping, loans, schemes, grants and investors
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Choose the right source of money for your stage, find the main government schemes on official sources, and avoid dangerous debt. **Time:** about 4 hours (1.5 hours study, 2.5 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Most micro-businesses don't need outside money to start, and this course is designed so that you won't. But when you need equipment or stock to grow, choose carefully: the wrong money can sink a good business.

### The funding ladder

Use the lowest rung that works:

1. **Customers' money:** advances, pre-orders, deposits, subscriptions paid upfront. It is free, and it proves demand.
2. **Bootstrapping:** your profits and your own risk money. Slow, but safe.
3. **Friends and family:** only with a written note of the amount, whether it is a loan or a gift, the repayment dates and what happens if the business fails. Unwritten family loans damage relationships.
4. **Bank loans,** often under government schemes (below).
5. **Grants and competitions:** free money with conditions, mostly for innovation.
6. **Angel investors and venture capital:** money for a share of your company. Only for businesses that can grow very fast; most micro-businesses should never raise it.

### Government schemes (check current rules)

| Scheme | What it offers | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **PM Mudra Yojana (PMMY)** | Loans for non-farm micro and small enterprises, through banks, NBFCs and microfinance institutions | Shishu up to ₹50,000; Kishore ₹50,000–₹5 lakh; Tarun ₹5–10 lakh; Tarun Plus ₹10–20 lakh for borrowers who repaid a Tarun loan. MUDRA says it uses no agents or middlemen. |
| **PMEGP** (run through KVIC) | A bank loan with a margin-money subsidy of 15–35% of the project cost, for new units | Project cost up to ₹50 lakh (manufacturing) or ₹20 lakh (business or service); own contribution 10% (5% for special categories); age 18+, Class VIII pass for larger projects; existing units not eligible. Apply on the PMEGP e-portal. |
| **CGTMSE** | Credit guarantees, so lenders can give micro and small enterprises loans without collateral | You apply through your bank; CGTMSE itself doesn't lend. |
| **Stand-Up India** | Bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for new (greenfield) enterprises | For SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, in manufacturing, services or trading. |
| **Kerala: Margin Money Grant to Nano Units** | A grant for new nano units with a project cost up to ₹10 lakh | 30% of project cost up to ₹3 lakh (40% up to ₹4 lakh for special categories); needs a bank loan of at least 40%; covers manufacturing, food processing, job work and services. Apply through the Taluk Industries Office. |
| **Kerala: Entrepreneur Support Scheme** | Investment support for manufacturing MSMEs | Manufacturing only; service units are not eligible. |
| **KSUM innovation grants** | Grants in stages for innovative startups registered with KSUM | Amounts change between rounds. The Startup India page on Kerala's policy lists up to ₹2 lakh (idea), ₹7 lakh (productisation) and ₹12 lakh (scale-up); check KSUM's grant portal for the current call. |
| **Startup India** | DPIIT recognition, the Seed Fund scheme and more | For eligible registered startups working on innovation. |

Your District Industries Centre (DIC) and Taluk Industries Office help with these schemes, including project reports, and the MSME Clinic at every DIC offers expert advice.

### Debt safety rules

- Borrow only for something that will produce income, and only after you have evidence of demand.
- Make sure the monthly payment (EMI) could be paid from other income if sales are slow for a few months.
- Compare the total cost (interest, processing fees, insurance), not just the EMI.
- Never borrow from private lenders who charge daily or weekly interest ("blade" lenders), never pledge gold to start a business, and never use a loan app you can't confirm is linked to an RBI-regulated lender.
- **Never pay an agent to "get" you a scheme loan or subsidy.** Apply yourself through the official portal, your bank or the DIC.

### Investors: only for fast-growing startups

Angel investors and venture capital funds buy a share of your company in exchange for money. They expect very fast growth and a big exit, which suits a tech startup, not a bakery or a local service. If that is your path, Y Combinator's talk on fundraising and its seed fundraising guide explain how it works, and KSUM runs investor events.

## Local example

Nisha wants a bigger oven and a stand mixer before next Christmas, about ₹45,000 in all. Her options:

| Option | Cost | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Christmas advances (50% of about 40 orders) | Free | Low, but the money arrives only when the orders do |
| Savings within her risk limit (₹10,000) | Free | Low |
| A Mudra Shishu loan from her bank (₹25,000) | The bank's interest rate, plus any fees | Medium: the EMI is due even in the monsoon slump |
| A gold loan | Interest, with the family's gold at risk | High |
| A private "blade" lender | Very high interest | Very high |

She chose ₹10,000 of savings, ₹10,000 from advances and a ₹25,000 Mudra Shishu loan, after checking that she could pay the EMI from her part-time salary if sales dropped. She applied directly at her bank's branch with her Udyam certificate, cash book and bank statements, and paid no agent.

Arun needs no loan: his costs are bus fares and data. He is bootstrapping, and will only consider a loan if he hires a helper who needs a laptop.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [MUDRA: Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana](https://www.mudra.org.in/) | Read the home page, especially the warning about agents | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [PIB: Mudra loan limit raised, Tarun Plus category (PDF)](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2024/oct/doc20241029426401.pdf) | Read the loan categories and the Tarun Plus limit | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [SBI: PMEGP scheme details](https://sbi.bank.in/web/business/sme/sme-government-schemes/pmegp) | Read the eligibility, project cost and subsidy | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [PMEGP e-portal (KVIC)](https://www.kviconline.gov.in/pmegpeportal/pmegphome/index.jsp) | The official application portal; type the address yourself and check it is the KVIC site | 5 min | unverified: the site blocks automated checks |
| [CGTMSE: credit guarantees for collateral-free loans](https://www.cgtmse.in/) | Read what a credit guarantee is, and that it works only through lenders | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Stand-Up India](https://www.standupmitra.in/) | Read who is eligible | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Kerala: Margin Money Grant to Nano Units](https://industry.kerala.gov.in/index.php/schemes-mainmenu/margin-money-grand-to-nano-units-schemes) | Read the grant, the funding pattern and how to apply | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Kerala: Entrepreneur Support Scheme (manufacturing units)](https://industry.kerala.gov.in/index.php/schemes-mainmenu/entrepreneur-support-scheme-schemes) | Read only if you plan a manufacturing unit | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Startup India: Kerala state startup policy](https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/sih/en/startup-scheme/state-startup-policies/Kerala-state-policy.html) | Read the part on KSUM grants | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [YC: "How Startup Fundraising Works" (Brad Flora)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zBUhQPPS9AY) | Only if you are building a fast-growing startup | about 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Write down your funding need: how much, for what, by when, and how it will increase your income.
2. List at least three ways to fund it from the funding ladder, with the cost and risk of each.
3. Read the official pages for the one or two schemes that might fit you, and note the eligibility and documents.
4. Visit or call your bank's MSME desk, your Taluk Industries Office or the DIC in Kozhikode, and ask one specific question about one scheme. Record the answer, the person's role and the date.
5. Decide: fund it now (and how), wait until you have more evidence or savings, or don't spend it at all.

**Proof to record:** Your funding need, the options comparison, your notes from the bank or DIC conversation, and your decision.

## Template: funding plan

```
FUNDING PLAN
What I need: ₹____ for ____ by ____
How it increases income: ____________
Evidence of demand: ____________

OPTIONS
Option | Amount | Cost (interest, fees) | Risk | Monthly payment
Customer advances |
Own savings (within my risk limit) |
Family (written note) |
Bank / Mudra / scheme |
Grant |

EMI CHECK
Monthly EMI: ₹____
Could I pay it from other income for 3 slow months? Y / N

SCHEME ENQUIRY
Where: bank MSME desk / Taluk Industries Office / DIC
Person's role: ____  Date: ____
Question: ____________
Answer: ____________
Documents needed: ____________

DECISION: fund now / wait / don't spend
```

## Common mistakes

- **Borrowing before proving demand.** A loan for a product nobody has paid for is a bet with borrowed money. Pre-sell first.
- **Starting a business because of a subsidy.** A subsidy can't save a business without customers. Decide on demand first, then look for support.
- **Paying agents.** MUDRA says it has no agents, and Udyam registration is free. Apply yourself through official channels.
- **Looking only at the EMI.** Compare the total cost, including fees, and make sure you can pay in a bad month.
- **Giving away equity casually.** A share of your company given to a friend for a small amount is hard to undo. Get advice before you offer any.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is the cheapest source of money for a new micro-business?
    - A) A gold loan
    - B) Customer advances and pre-orders
    - C) A blade lender
    - D) A credit card balance
2. What does Mudra's Shishu category cover? (Check current rules.)
    - A) Loans up to ₹50,000
    - B) Loans of ₹5–10 lakh
    - C) Loans of ₹10–20 lakh
    - D) Loans above ₹1 crore
3. Someone offers to get you a PMEGP loan for a ₹5,000 "processing fee". What should you do?
    - A) Pay quickly
    - B) Refuse, and apply yourself through the official portal, your bank or the DIC
    - C) Pay half now
    - D) Ask for a receipt and pay
4. Who is Kerala's Entrepreneur Support Scheme for?
    - A) All businesses
    - B) Manufacturing MSMEs only
    - C) Service units only
    - D) Students only
5. Who are venture capital investors a good fit for?
    - A) Most home bakeries
    - B) Fast-growing, scalable startups
    - C) Every new business
    - D) People with a poor credit record

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the official scheme pages for Mudra, PMEGP, CGTMSE, Stand-Up India and Kerala's nano-unit grant (about 1.5 hours)
- **Action:** write your funding need, compare options, ask your bank or DIC about one scheme and decide. It is done when your proof is saved: your funding need, the options comparison, your notes from the bank or DIC conversation, and your decision.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** It costs nothing and proves that people want what you sell.
2. **A.** Kishore covers ₹50,000–₹5 lakh, Tarun ₹5–10 lakh and Tarun Plus ₹10–20 lakh.
3. **B.** Scheme applications don't need paid agents; such offers are a common scam.
4. **B.** The scheme page puts service enterprises on its negative list.
5. **B.** VCs need very fast growth to make their returns; most small businesses don't aim for that.

sections.title: Module 9: Legal and compliance
sections.summary: Legal work sounds frightening, but for a micro-business most of it is simple: choose the right structure, register what your activity needs, put agreements in writing, protect your name and treat customers and their data fairly. This module walks through each, using official sources, and ends with a compliance checklist for your own business.
sections.content:
## Overview

Legal work sounds frightening, but for a micro-business most of it is simple: choose the right structure, register what your activity needs, put agreements in writing, protect your name and treat customers and their data fairly. This module walks through each, using official sources, and ends with a compliance checklist for your own business.

This is general information, not legal advice. Rules differ by activity and change often, so every rule here is marked check current rules. Confirm anything important with a lawyer, a CA or the office concerned.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Compare sole proprietorship, partnership, LLP, OPC and private limited company, and choose one for now
- List the registrations and licences your business needs in Kerala, and do the free, simple ones yourself
- Use a simple written agreement or terms of sale with a fair refund policy
- Protect your name and content, and follow consumer, advertising and data protection basics

## Time

About 12 hours in total: 10 hours of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 22–23.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M09-L01: Choose a business structure (about 3 hours)
2. ENT-M09-L02: Registrations and licences in Kerala (about 3 hours)
3. ENT-M09-L03: Contracts, IP, consumer and digital law basics (about 4 hours)

## Module project: Compliance checklist and legal pack

1. Your structure decision, with reasons (L01).
2. Your compliance checklist: every registration and licence, whether it is needed, status, renewal date and official link (L02).
3. Your one-page agreement or terms of sale, with a refund policy (L03).
4. The privacy notice on your order or enquiry form (L03).
5. Your trademark search result for your business name (L03).
6. Show the checklist to someone who knows the rules (a DIC officer, a CA or an experienced business owner) and note any corrections.

**Proof to record:** The Founder Toolkit/09 Legal folder with these documents, and your filled Compliance tab.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Not considered | Chosen without comparing | Compared, with reasons, and a partner agreement if needed |
| Registrations | Unknown | Listed, but not checked with official sources | Checked with official sources; free ones done; renewal dates set |
| Agreements | Nothing in writing | WhatsApp messages only | A one-page agreement or terms, with a refund policy |
| Name and content | Not checked | Checked on Google only | Trademark search done; only own or licensed content |
| Customer data | Collected freely | Some care taken | Minimum data, a privacy notice, consent and safe storage |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: read the comparison table and stay a sole proprietor unless you have a partner or an investor.
- L02: do Udyam (if you are selling) and confirm your local licence.
- L03: write a five-line refund policy and a three-line privacy notice.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Registering a company too early.** Compliance costs add up; start simple and change when there is a reason.
- **Paying agents for free registrations.** Udyam registration is free on the official portal.
- **Borrowing someone else's licence or GST number.** Never. Get your own registrations.

tasks.text: Module project: Compliance checklist and legal pack
tasks.detail: **Proof to record:** The Founder Toolkit/09 Legal folder with these documents, and your filled Compliance tab.

tasks.text: Self-assessment: rubric scored, no row at 1

sections.title: ENT-M09-L01: Choose a business structure
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare the five common business structures in India and choose the right one for now, with a written agreement if you have a partner. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour study (plus 35 minutes if you have a co-founder), 2 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A business structure decides who owns the business, who is responsible for its debts, how it is taxed and how much paperwork it needs. For a new micro-business, simpler is usually better, and you can change structure later when there is a reason.

| | Sole proprietorship | Partnership firm | LLP | One Person Company (OPC) | Private limited company |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Owners | One person | 2 or more partners | 2 or more partners, at least 2 of them designated partners | One person, with a nominee | 2 or more shareholders and directors |
| Main law | No special law: it is you, trading | Indian Partnership Act, 1932 | LLP Act, 2008 | Companies Act, 2013 | Companies Act, 2013 |
| Registration | None as such; you use Udyam, GST and licences as needed | A partnership deed; registering with the Registrar of Firms is optional but useful | With the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) | With the MCA | With the MCA |
| Liability | Unlimited: your personal property is at risk | Unlimited, and shared | Limited to your contribution (not for your own fraud) | Limited | Limited |
| Paperwork | Lowest | Low | Medium: yearly filings | High: company compliance | Highest |
| Raising equity | Not possible | Hard | Possible, but investors prefer companies | Limited | Easiest; most investors need it |
| Good for | Starting small and testing | Two or more people starting small together | Partners who want limited liability with less paperwork than a company | A single founder who needs a company | Startups planning to raise investment or grow fast |

Points to know (check current rules):

- **Partnership firms:** under section 69 of the Partnership Act, an unregistered firm generally can't sue a third party to enforce a contract. Registering with the Registrar of Firms (in Kerala, under the Registration Department) avoids this problem.
- **Startup India recognition** (by DPIIT) is for private limited companies, registered partnership firms, LLPs and cooperative societies. A sole proprietorship can't be recognised as a startup.
- **Tax** differs between structures. Ask a CA before you choose anything other than a sole proprietorship.
- **Costs:** an LLP or a company needs digital signatures, government fees, professional help and yearly filings. Don't take that on until you need limited liability, investors, or a bigger client who insists on it.

### If you have a co-founder or partner

Write your agreement down before you start, even with a friend or relative. Cover:

1. **Roles:** who does what
2. **Money:** who puts in how much, and whether it is a loan or ownership
3. **Ownership split**, and **vesting**: ownership earned over time, so someone who leaves early doesn't keep a big share
4. **Decisions:** how they are made, and how a tie is broken
5. **Pay:** when and how partners take money out
6. **Assets:** who owns the brand, the content and the customer list
7. **Leaving:** what happens if someone leaves or wants to sell
8. **Disputes:** how they will be resolved

Y Combinator's talk on co-founder relationships covers choosing a co-founder and keeping the relationship healthy.

## Local example

Arun works with his friend Fazil, who photographs stock for some shops. They thought about a partnership but kept ShopAssist as **Arun's sole proprietorship** for now, paying Fazil ₹300 per shop as a freelancer, agreed in writing. If they later share ownership, they will write a partnership deed with vesting and register the firm, or form an LLP if clients or risks grow.

Nisha runs Nisha's Oven as a **sole proprietorship**: she is the only owner, her risks are small and the paperwork is the lowest.

Fathima and her cousin want to turn PSC Sprint into an app and apply to KSUM. They plan to form a **private limited company** once their weekly test channel proves demand, because startup recognition needs a registered entity and investors would expect a company.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 13](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/13-introduction) | Sections 13.1 and 13.3–13.5 on business structures. The book uses US law, so read it for the ideas only | 45 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA): LLPs and companies](https://www.mca.gov.in/) | Browse the portal to see where LLPs and companies are registered (check current rules) | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (India Code, PDF)](https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/12849/1/the_indian_partnership_act_1932.pdf) | Optional: section 69, on what happens when a firm is not registered | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [Startup India: who is eligible for DPIIT startup recognition](https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/sih/en/startupgov/startup_recognition_page.html) | Read the eligibility criteria for startup recognition | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |
| [YC: "Keys To Successful Co-Founder Relationships"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A4SLDQDXdp0) | Only if you have, or want, a co-founder | about 35 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Fill in the structure decision sheet for your business.
2. Write down what would make you change structure later: hiring staff, a large contract, raising money, a partner joining.
3. If you have a partner or co-founder, draft your one-page agreement covering the 8 points, and sign it together.
4. Ask one CA, lawyer or experienced business owner one question about your choice, and note the answer.
5. Save the decision in Founder Toolkit/09 Legal.

**Proof to record:** Your structure decision sheet, your triggers for changing structure, the partner agreement (if you have a partner) and the expert's answer.

## Template: structure decision

```
STRUCTURE DECISION     Date: ____
Owners: ____ (how many, and who)
Could customers or suppliers hold me liable for large
amounts? Y / N  ____________
Do I plan to raise equity from investors? Y / N
Do I need Startup India or KSUM recognition? Y / N
Paperwork I can handle: low / medium / high

Choice for now: sole proprietorship / partnership /
LLP / OPC / private limited company
Why (3 reasons): ____________
I will review this when:
[ ] I hire staff  [ ] turnover passes ₹____
[ ] a partner joins  [ ] I raise money
[ ] a client insists
Question asked to (CA / lawyer / owner): ____
Answer: ____________
```

## Template: co-founder or partner agreement

```
PARTNER AGREEMENT (one page, signed by everyone)
1. Roles: ____ does ____; ____ does ____
2. Money in: ____ (a loan, or ownership?)
3. Ownership split: ____ / ____
   Vesting: earned over ____ years, ____ each year
4. Decisions: ____; ties broken by ____
5. Taking money out: ____
6. The brand, content and customer list belong to ____
7. If someone leaves: ____
8. Disputes: talk first, then ____
   (mediation or arbitration)
Signed: ____  ____    Date: ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Registering a company too early.** A company brings yearly filings and professional fees. Start as a sole proprietor unless you have a clear reason not to.
- **No written agreement with a partner.** Friends and relatives fall out over money and roles. Write it down while you still agree.
- **A 50/50 split with no vesting.** If one partner leaves after two months and keeps half, the business is stuck. Use vesting.
- **Following a US article.** OpenStax explains the ideas using US law. Check Indian rules on official sites or with a professional.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which structure has the least paperwork?
    - A) Private limited company
    - B) Sole proprietorship
    - C) LLP
    - D) One Person Company
2. What is the main risk of a sole proprietorship?
    - A) It needs seven directors
    - B) Unlimited liability: your personal property is at risk
    - C) It can't open a bank account
    - D) It can't sell online
3. What can an unregistered partnership firm generally not do, under section 69?
    - A) Sell goods
    - B) Sue a third party to enforce a contract
    - C) Hire staff
    - D) Open a shop
4. Which kinds of entity can get DPIIT startup recognition?
    - A) Only sole proprietorships
    - B) Private limited companies, registered partnership firms, LLPs and cooperative societies
    - C) Any individual
    - D) Only government companies
5. Why use vesting in a co-founder agreement?
    - A) To pay less tax
    - B) So ownership is earned over time, and someone who leaves early doesn't keep a big share
    - C) Every business must
    - D) To raise prices

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapter 13 (for the ideas), the MCA portal and Startup India's eligibility page (about 1 hour)
- **Action:** choose your structure with reasons, set review triggers, write a partner agreement if needed and ask an expert. It is done when your proof is saved: your structure decision sheet, your triggers for changing structure, the partner agreement (if you have a partner) and the expert's answer.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** There is no separate registration law; you trade as yourself.
2. **B.** You and the business are legally the same, so its debts are your debts.
3. **B.** Registration with the Registrar of Firms removes this limit.
4. **B.** That is the list on Startup India's recognition page.
5. **B.** Vesting protects the people who stay and keep building.

Action: choose your structure with reasons, set review triggers, write a partner agreement if needed and ask an expert
tasks.detail: **Proof to record:** Your structure decision sheet, your triggers for changing structure, the partner agreement (if you have a partner) and the expert's answer. Paste the link to your proof (a Google Drive file, sheet or photo) in this task's note.

sections.title: ENT-M09-L02: Registrations and licences in Kerala
sections.summary: **Outcome:** List the registrations and licences your business needs in Kerala, do the free and simple ones yourself, and avoid agents who charge for free services. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour 15 minutes study, 1 hour 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Which registrations you need depends on what you do, where you do it and how big you are. These are the common ones for a small business in Kerala. Check each one against the official source for your exact activity (check current rules).

### The basics

- **PAN, Aadhaar and a bank account** for the business.
- **Udyam registration (MSME):** free, online, paperless and based on self-declaration, using your Aadhaar, with PAN and GST details linked where required. The portal warns against fake websites and says no private agency is authorised to do MSME registration. Udyam opens the door to MSME schemes and priority-sector loans. Under the limits shown on the portal, a micro enterprise has investment up to ₹2.5 crore and turnover up to ₹10 crore.
- **GST registration:** only if your turnover crosses the threshold or a compulsory case applies (ENT-M08-L03).

### The local body licence

Most trades and businesses need a licence from the local body: the **grama panchayat** in villages, or the **municipality or corporation** in towns. Kerala's **K-SMART** system runs local body services online. It started in municipalities and corporations in January 2024, and grama panchayats have been moving their services onto it; one panchayat's website now says it accepts applications only through K-SMART, either directly or through Akshaya centres. Ask your panchayat's front office which licence your activity needs, the fee, and whether a home-based activity is covered.

### The Kerala MSME Facilitation Act and K-SWIFT

Under the **Kerala Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Facilitation Act, 2019**, an MSME that is not in the Pollution Control Board's "red" category can file a self-certification and receive a **Certificate of in-principle approval**. It is valid for **three years and six months**: you must obtain the required approvals within that time, and during it no authority may inspect you for the purpose of those approvals. **K-SWIFT** is Kerala's online single-window system for clearances. In 2023, the Supreme Court held that once such a certificate was obtained, a separate permission under the Kerala Panchayat Raj Act was not needed during its validity. Ask your DIC or Taluk Industries Office whether this route suits your unit.

### Food businesses: FSSAI

Every food business needs **FSSAI registration or a licence**. Small food businesses, including home-based ones, with turnover up to ₹12 lakh a year need only **basic registration**, at ₹100 a year; above that, a state licence is required (check current rules). Applications go through FSSAI's FoSCoS portal. Packed products also need proper labels under the FSSAI and legal metrology rules: the maker's name and address, net quantity, MRP, date of manufacture, best-before date and consumer care details.

### When you hire or open premises

- **Kerala Shops and Commercial Establishments Act:** if you open a shop or office, or employ workers, check with the Labour Department whether you must register.
- **EPF and ESI:** these apply once you employ a certain number of people. Check the current rules with EPFO and ESIC.
- **Professional tax:** collected by local bodies from people in trades and professions above certain income levels.
- **Pollution Control Board consent:** needed for some manufacturing activities.

### Don't pay agents for free services

Udyam registration is free. MUDRA says it has no agents. Many official services can be done online yourself, or at an Akshaya centre for its usual service charge. Be wary of websites that look official but charge "registration fees", and of messages saying your registration will be "cancelled" unless you pay.

## Local example

**Nisha's checklist:** Udyam registration (free; she did it herself online in about 15 minutes); FSSAI basic registration, since her turnover is under ₹12 lakh (₹100 a year); a call to her grama panchayat's front office to ask whether her home bakery needs a licence, with the answer and date written down; labels for her packed plum cakes showing her name and address, net weight, price, date of manufacture, best-before date and phone number. No GST registration yet.

**Arun's checklist:** Udyam registration (free); no FSSAI, as he sells no food; no GST yet. The panchayat told him that his home-based service didn't need a licence, but that an office would; he noted the answer, the officer's role and the date.

**Fathima's checklist:** Udyam is optional for now. Her main legal care is copyright: every question in her packs is her own (next lesson).

## Free resources

| [FSSAI FoSCoS portal (apply online)](https://foscos.fssai.gov.in/) | Only for food businesses: the application portal; type the address yourself and check it is the FSSAI site | 5 min | unverified: the site blocks automated checks |
| [IKM: what K-SMART covers](https://ikm.gov.in/en/node/1103) | Read what K-SMART covers | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

| [Kerala MSME Facilitation Act, 2019 (India Code, PDF)](https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/21022/1/act16_of_2019_engfinal.pdf) | Optional: sections 5 and 6, on self-certification and the in-principle approval certificate (check current rules) | 15 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

| [Department of Consumer Affairs: label rules for packaged goods (PDF)](https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/02-Aug-2024.pdf) | Only if you sell packed goods: the label declarations | 5 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Fill in the compliance checklist below for your business: for each item, whether it is needed, how to get it, the cost, the official link, the status and the renewal date.
2. If you are already selling, do your Udyam registration yourself on the official portal. It is free.
3. Call or visit your grama panchayat or municipality front office and ask which licence your activity needs, the fee and the process. Note the answer, the officer's role and the date.
4. If you sell food, start your FSSAI registration or licence.
5. Put every renewal date in your calendar, and save a copy of every certificate in Founder Toolkit/09 Legal.

**Proof to record:** Your filled Compliance tab, your Udyam certificate (if you are selling), notes from the local body with the date, and any applications you started.

```csv

```

## Common mistakes

- **Paying agents for free registrations.** Udyam registration is free on the official portal, which says no agency is authorised to do it for you.
- **Assuming a home business needs nothing.** Food businesses need FSSAI registration even at home, and some activities need a local licence. Ask, and write down the answer.
- **Missing renewals.** Licences expire. Put every renewal date in your calendar.
- **Using someone else's licence or GST number.** It is illegal and puts both of you at risk. Get your own.
- **Trusting one website.** Rules vary by activity and place. Confirm with the office concerned, and note the date.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. How much does Udyam registration cost on the official portal?
    - A) ₹2,999
    - B) Nothing: it is free
    - C) ₹500 a year
    - D) ₹100
2. What does a home baker with ₹4 lakh annual turnover need from FSSAI? (Check current rules.)
    - A) Nothing
    - B) Basic FSSAI registration
    - C) A central FSSAI licence
    - D) Only GST
3. How long is Kerala's Certificate of in-principle approval valid?
    - A) 6 months
    - B) 1 year
    - C) 3 years and 6 months
    - D) Forever
4. Which system now handles Kerala local body services, including trade licences, online?
    - A) K-SMART
    - B) Udyam
    - C) The GST portal
    - D) The MCA portal
5. A website says: "Your Udyam certificate will be cancelled. Pay a ₹2,500 renewal fee today." What is it likely to be?
    - A) A real government notice
    - B) A scam: Udyam registration is free
    - C) A tax refund
    - D) A loan offer

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the Udyam, K-SMART and K-SWIFT pages, plus the FSSAI and legal metrology pages if you sell food or packed goods (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

It is done when your proof is saved: your filled Compliance tab, your Udyam certificate (if you are selling), notes from the local body with the date, and any applications you started.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** The portal says registration is totally free.
2. **B.** Basic registration covers food businesses with turnover up to ₹12 lakh.
3. **C.** Section 6 of the Kerala MSME Facilitation Act sets three years and six months.
4. **A.** K-SMART covers business licences, building permits, certificates and more.
5. **B.** Official Udyam registration has no fee; scammers copy official-looking pages.
